entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• a record of the ancestors: This phrase introduces Matthew 1:1–17. A similar phrase appears in Genesis to start each section of that book. 

• Jesus … David … Abraham: These names repeat in reverse order in the list of Jesus' ancestors. This is a literary form called chiasm (arrangement of elements in mirror-image). Identifying Jesus as a descendant of David introduces him as the Messiah (see Matthew 12:23; Matthew 22:42–45). The link to Abraham emphasizes God's promise to Israel and how the covenant (agreement) extends to include all nations (see Matthew 28:16–20; Genesis 12:3).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
This story shows how certain parts of the life of Jesus fulfilled Old Testament prophecies. This includes: 

• his family history and birth (chapter Matthew 1:1), and 

• the places he lived as a child (chapter Matthew 2:2). 

The story also shows how efforts to stop the plan of God do not work (Matthew 2:1–15; see also Matthew 27:62–66).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Rahab was a Gentile prostitute who risked her life to hide the two spies of Joshua in Jericho (Joshua 2:1–21). Her place in the Messiah's family tree emphasizes the grace of God. She is praised for her faith in Israel's God and her good actions (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Asa (Greek Asaph): this likely refers to the Old Testament king (1 Kings 15:9–24; 1 Chronicles 3:10) and not the psalmist Asaph (1 Chronicles 6:39; 1 Chronicles 25:1–2; Psalms 50, Psalms 73:73–83). Matthew focuses on the family line from David to the Messiah.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: father of (or ancestor of): Here this term refers to multiple generations (2 Chronicles 21:1–26:1). The same is true for Josiah (Matthew 1:11) and Shealtiel (Matthew 1:12). The family line skips Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah (2 Kings 8:24; 1 Chronicles 3:11; 2 Chronicles 22:1, 2 Chronicles 22:11; 2 Chronicles 24:27). Perhaps this is because of their connection to Ahab and Jezebel.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: father: Josiah was Jehoiachin's grandfather.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Shealtiel: Refer to 1 Chronicles 3:17–19 and Ezra 3:2.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Old Testament is clearly the source for Matthew 1:1–11. Matthew probably also used royal records and oral traditions for Matthew 1:12–16.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This family history follows Joseph, who is part of the family line of King David (see also study note on Luke 3:23–38).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
Matthew says each time period has fourteen generations. But the first and third periods list only thirteen. A traditional Jewish and Old Testament method would count King David in both the first and second groups. It would include Jesus in the third group. 

This suggests Matthew is probably emphasizing the gematria (a system where letters represent numbers). The letters in the Hebrew word dawid (meaning "David") add up to fourteen. Matthew is emphasizing Jesus’ credentials as the Messiah (Matthew 1:1).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Jesus Christ (literally Jesus the Christ): Christ is not a personal name. Christ is a title that means "Messiah" or "God's chosen one."

• pledged in marriage: In Judaism, engagement (or betrothal) was a permanent relationship (Malachi 2:14). It could only end through legal action. So, by law, Mary was Joseph’s wife and he was her husband (see Matthew 1:20; Deuteronomy 22:23–24). This was true even though they had not had sexual relations. Since Mary was a virgin when the Holy Spirit conceived Jesus, it proves Jesus’ divine nature.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Joseph was a righteous man. This means he obeyed the law (see Luke 1:6). He reconsidered marrying Mary because it appeared she had committed adultery. He could have cleared his name by publicly accusing Mary. This would have led to her trial and possible execution (Deuteronomy 22:23–27; compare Numbers 5:11–31). Or he could pay a fine and end the engagement (see also Mishnah Sotah 1:1–5). Joseph chose to be kind and decided to end the engagement quietly.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The angel of the Lord told Joseph in a dream (see Matthew 2:12–13, Matthew 2:19, Matthew 2:22) that no one had seduced or harmed Mary. Instead, the baby was conceived by the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:34–35). The Holy Spirit often plays a creative and life-giving role (Genesis 1:2; Ezekiel 37:1–14; John 3:5–8).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Jesus is the Greek version of the Hebrew name Yeshua, which means "The Lord saves." This name describes his role, that he will save his people from their sins. 

• His people may refer to either Israel as a nation (Matthew 2:6) or to the Messiah’s people, the church. This includes both Jews and non-Jewish (Gentile) people (Matthew 4:15–16; Matthew 16:18; Matthew 28:18–20).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus being born from a virgin fulfills Isaiah 7:14. The Hebrew word ‘almah can mean “virgin” or “young woman.” In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it was translated as parthenos (“virgin”), which Matthew quotes. Matthew sees the ‘almah in Isaiah as pointing forward to the Virgin Mary.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• he had no union with her until she gave birth to a Son: this might indicate that Joseph had sexual relations with Mary after Jesus was born. (Some traditions teach that Mary remained a virgin throughout her life.)

• Joseph named him Jesus, showing he accepted the child as his own.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Bethlehem was King David’s hometown (1 Samuel 16:1–13; John 7:42). 

• King Herod was also called "Herod the Great." He had a rapid increase in power. He went from being the governor of Galilee to the king of Galilee, Judea, and Samaria. He was king from 37–4 BC. He was very loyal to Rome. He was famous for impressive building projects. This included a major renovation of the Temple in Jerusalem. His rule also included family conflicts, suspicion, and the murder of his own family members and innocent children (Josephus, Antiquities 15.7.1–5; Matthew 2:16–18).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
The wise men's focus on the star shows they were astrologers. Their knowledge of the Old Testament (possibly Numbers 24:17) suggests they came from Babylonia, where many Jews lived. These men were Gentiles (non-Jewish people), which hints at God accepting Gentiles in his kingdom (Matthew 8:11–12; Matthew 15:21–28; Matthew 28:16–20). 

All through the Gospel, unlikely Gentiles worship the Jewish Messiah, while many Jewish leaders (Herod, the high priests, the teachers of religious law, and the Pharisees) oppose him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Matthew often describes Jesus as receiving worshipped (Matthew 2:2, Matthew 2:8, Matthew 2:11; Matthew 8:2; Matthew 9:18; Matthew 14:33; Matthew 15:25; Matthew 20:20; Matthew 28:9, Matthew 28:17). In this way, Matthew identifies Jesus as God.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: It worried Herod very much because he thought this child might challenge him as King of the Jews.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The leading priests had political and religious influence and mainly served in the temple (see Matthew 21:23). Herod gathered the teachers of religious law because they knew Old Testament prophecies and were often influential Pharisees.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Bethlehem was a small village. It was important because it was where King David was born. The religious leaders knew from prophecy (Matthew 1:22) that this is where God would cause his Messiah to be born there. 

• King David had been a shepherd when he was young. As king, he became the shepherd of Israel (2 Samuel 5:2). Micah 5:2–4 predicts the Messiah as a shepherd (compare Psalm 23:1).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: God placed the star to guide the wise men to the Messiah (see Numbers 24:17). The details are unclear.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The wise men gave costly gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the king (see Psalm 72:10–17; Isaiah 60). The idea of three wise men comes from the number of gifts. But the text does not say how many wise men there were.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: flee to Egypt … until I tell you: This action fulfills the prophecy in Hosea 11:1 (refer to study note on Matthew 4:1–11; see also Genesis 15:13–16; Genesis 46:1–5; Exodus 15:1–21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Out of Egypt I called My Son: See Hosea 11:1, which refers to when God led the Israelites out of Egypt.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Put to death all the boys: Herod was famous for his cruelty. He even killed his own son to protect his throne. This led to the saying, “It is safer to be Herod’s pig [Greek hus] than his son [Greek huios].” This is because Herod followed Jewish kosher laws. 

• two years old and under: Herod estimated the child's age based on the wise men’s report.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Ramah was a village near Bethlehem. It is where the patriarch Jacob buried his wife Rachel (Genesis 35:18–20; Jeremiah 31:15–17).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: After Herod died: Herod the Great died in 4 BC. Caesar (the Roman emperor) divided his kingdom. Herod's son Archelaus (Matthew 2:22) became ruler of Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. Herod Antipas (Matthew 14:1–12; Luke 13:31–32) took charge of Galilee and Perea.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus returned to Israel to fulfill the prophecy in Hosea 11:1 (see Hosea 2:13–15).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Archelaus, like his father, ruled with cruelty, injustice, and harshness. 

• Joseph moved to Galilee to escape the control of Archelaus. This fulfilled a prophecy (see Matthew 4:12–16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: “He will be called a Nazarene”: Matthew connects the name Nazareth with words from the prophets (see Isaiah 11:1, where the Messiah is called a “Branch,” [Hebrew netser]; and Judges 13:5, where Samson is called a “Nazirite”).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• John the Baptist announced the arrival of Jesus (see Mark 1:1–11; Luke 3:1–22; John 1:6–8, John 1:19–34). John helped people get ready to welcome him (Matt 3:3). John drew large crowds (Matthew 3:5) and gathered a group of followers (Matthew 9:14). This group continued for a short time as a movement, even after the Christian church began (see Acts 18:24–28). 

• John lived in the Judean wilderness. This was symbolic because the wilderness linked to God giving the law (see Exodus 19:1). It also related to God's final redemption of Israel at the end of time (see Isaiah 40:3).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The prophetic call to return to God means turning away from pride and sin and choosing humble obedience to God (compare Isaiah 1:16–20 and Jeremiah 3:11–22). John’s message included specific practical advice (Luke 3:11–14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Isaiah talked about someone making a path in the desert for God to come back to Israel (Isaiah 40:1–11). John's work got things ready for Jesus to arrive (see Matthew 11:10; compare John 12:41).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: John wore the same kind of clothes and ate the same kind of food as Elijah, a prophet who had lived many years before (2 Kings 1:8; Malachi 4:5; Sirach 48:10–11).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• John's ministry became so popular that many people from Jerusalem and Judea came to hear him. 

• Confessing their sins: Those who listened to John's preaching and turned away from sin were ready to accept the ministry of Jesus (Luke 7:27, Luke 7:29). 

• they were baptized: John's practice of baptism might have started with the Old Testament idea of purification (see Isaiah 1:16; Isaiah 4:4; Ezekiel 36:25).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The Pahrisees' name comes from the Hebrew word perushim, which means separated ones or exact interpreters. 

• The Sadducees, a group of priests, probably got their name from Zadok the priest (2 Samuel 15:24–29; Ezekiel 44:10–16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance: John calls for action and real ethical change. Only talking about it is not enough (see Luke 3:10–14; compare Matthew 5:19–20, Matthew 5:46; Matthew 7:21; Matthew 23:3).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father’: Some people had wrong assumptions. They thought that being descendants of Abraham meant they were free from God's judgment. 

• A key theme in Matthew is that God will create new children of Abraham. He will include non-Jews (Gentiles) in God's people. He will remove Jews who reject the Messiah (see Matthew 8:11–12; Matthew 21:43; Matthew 22:1–14; Matthew 28:16–20; Romans 4:9–25; Galatians 3:6–14, Galatians 3:29).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• One more powerful than I: Even though he was popular and many people continued to follow him, John knew he was less important than the Messiah. 

• whose sandals I am not worthy to carry: In Jewish culture, removing and carrying sandals was a task for slaves. Not even a rabbi's disciple would do it. 

• with the Holy Spirit and with fire: This happened at Pentecost (see Joel 2:28–29; Acts 2:1–47). This may include the ministry of Jesus, empowered by the Holy Spirit (see Matthew 12:28; Luke 4:14). Fire could mean purification (Zech 13:9) or judgment (Malachi 3:2–3; 4:1; see Isaiah 1:25; Isaiah 4:4). It is a “Spirit-and-fire baptism.” The Messiah completes what John could only start (full judgment and purification).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
Farmers used a winnowing fork to throw harvested grain into the air, letting the useless husks (chaff) blow away. 

The Messiah's work separates humanity into two groups: 

• the wheat, those who respond and become God's new people; and

• the chaff, those who refuse to repent (see Matthew 3:8).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: John had already admitted (Matthew 3:11–12) that he was less important than the Messiah, so he felt unworthy to baptize him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: “It is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness in this way”: This means completing what the Old Testament required or prophesied (for example, Jeremiah 31:31–34). In Matthew, “righteousness” means acting according to God’s will (see Matthew 5:20; Matthew 6:1, Matthew 6:33; Matthew 21:32).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Spirit of God came down like a dove to anoint Jesus, who would bring salvation. This was similar to a king being anointed with oil at his crowning. The Holy Spirit gave Jesus the strength to achieve God's salvation and defeat Satan (see Matthew 12:18, Matthew 12:28). This same Spirit gives strength to the disciples of Jesus (Matthew 10:20; Acts 1:8).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• This is My beloved Son (see Psalm 2:7): The title “Son of God” explains the nature and role of Jesus (see Matthew 4:3, Matthew 4:6; Matthew 14:33; Matthew 16:16; Matthew 17:5; Matthew 26:63; Matthew 27:54; Matthew 28:19). In his special relationship with God the Father, Jesus achieves salvation as the faithful and obedient Son. 

• in whom I am well pleased: God the Father confirmed his Son’s work with words from Isaiah (Isaiah 42:1) and prepared Israel for the work of Jesus.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Jesus was led by the Spirit: God arranged this test to examine the Messiah’s character (see Deuteronomy 8:2). 

• to be tempted by the devil: God started this test of character, using the devil's wish to lead Jesus into sin. God tempts no one (James 1:13–14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
This story of the temptation of Jesus shows clear parallels between Adam and Jesus. Jesus is the second Adam (see Romans 5:12–19) and the second Israel (Matthew 2:15). Unlike the ancient Israelites, Jesus completed Israel’s history by wandering through the desert without sinning. He showed he was the obedient Son of God by defeating Satan in spiritual battle. 

Since Jesus faced temptation as a human, he can understand the temptations we encounter (see Hebrews 2:14–18; Hebrews 4:15). He helps us overcome them as he did (1 Corinthians 10:13).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Forty days and forty nights (see Exodus 24:18; Exodus 34:28; 1 Kings 19:8): God tested Israel for forty-years in the wilderness (Exodus 16:35; Deuteronomy 1:3).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus refused to use his supernatural power to get food, trusting God to provide it. The people of Israel relentlessly tested God with complaints and disbelief (see Exodus 16). But, Jesus refused to doubt God's faithfulness. Instead, he relied on God to meet his real need. This was the spiritual provision that comes from every word of God.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus refused to test God by assuming God would always protect him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: It is also written: Jesus responded to the devil's use of Scripture by emphasizing a more important principle (honoring God) which the devil ignored.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Satan is called "the prince of this world" in John 12:31. He offered Jesus control over all the world's kingdoms and their power. Satan did this to try to stop Jesus from fulfilling God's will. 

• Glory means political power and control (for example, Matthew 6:29). Satan planned to tempt Jesus to misuse his divine nature as Son. He wanted to distract him from the path of suffering and obedience that led to the crucifixion.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Then the devil left Him: Jesus rejected Satan. This points ahead to his later victories over demons (Matthew 12:28), Satan's defeat through the cross (Colossians 2:14–15), and the final victory at the end of time (Romans 16:20; Revelation 12:7–17; Revelation 20:2–3, Revelation 20:10). 

• Angels had already been part of the Messiah's arrival and protection (Matthew 1:20, Matthew 1:24; Matthew 2:13, Matthew 2:19). Now they came and cared for Jesus after his temptation, fulfilling the Old Testament (Matthew 4:6; see Psalm 91:11–12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Herod Antipas was the ruler of Galilee and Perea. He had arrested John the Baptist (see Matthew 14:1–12). John was probably working in the area at this time. 

• When Jesus heard about this, he left Judea. This was near Perea, where Herod had John arrested. Jesus then went back to Galilee. Jesus left to avoid death before he could finish his mission of revealing God's Kingdom. Like Joseph's escape to Nazareth (Matthew 2:22–23), avoiding danger can also be part of God's plan and fulfill prophecy (Matthew 4:14–16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: John the Baptist and the Father announced Jesus as the Messiah (Matthew 3:13–17). He then endured testing in the wilderness with obedience (Matthew 4:1–11). After this, the Messiah was ready to begin his work. He first preached the message of the kingdom of God to the people of Galilee.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Capernaum was in Galilee, a region that the religious leaders in Judea and Jerusalem viewed negatively (see John 1:46; John 7:41–42, John 7:52). Many people from Judea thought Galileans to be unrefined and poorly spoken (compare Matt 26:73). The leaders believed these people could make their teachings less accurate. Galilee also had more non-Jewish people than Judea.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus taught that the kingdom of heaven was coming soon and urged people to repent (stop doing what is wrong) in preparation (see Matthew 3:2; Matthew 10:7).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Simon, also known as Peter, became the leader of the apostles (see Matthew 14:28; Matthew 15:15; Matthew 16:16) and the representative disciple (Matthew 14:29–30; Matthew 16:15–19, Matthew 16:22–23).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The call of the first disciples shows one purpose of the ministry of Jesus: to invite people to follow him with self-denying obedience (compare Matthew 4:17, Matthew 4:23–25).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Come, follow Me: This meant accepting the beliefs and lifestyle of a teacher as your own (Matthew 16:24; Deuteronomy 5:33; 1 Kings 19:19–21). 

• fishers of men: The disciples would help in the saving and judging work of the kingdom of heaven (see Matthew 10:5–15; Matthew 13:47–51; Ezekiel 29:4–5; Amos 4:2).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: They left the boat and their father: To be disciples of Jesus required both commitment and sacrifice from the brothers (see Matthew 8:18–22; Matthew 10:38; Matthew 16:24; Matthew 19:21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The Messiah's work focuses on three main activities: teaching … preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing.

• The synagogues were Jewish places for prayer, study, and discussing Scripture and tradition. They were also the social centers of many Jewish villages. The hypocrisy and hostility of Jewish leaders were obvious in the synagogues (Matthew 6:2, Matthew 6:5; Matthew 10:17; Matthew 12:9–14; Matthew 13:54; Matthew 23:6, Matthew 23:34).

• Preaching the gospel involves sharing the message about the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 9:35; Matthew 24:14; Matthew 26:13; also Mark 1:1; Romans 1:16). This message often causes hostility (see Matthew 9:32–34; Matthew 10:27–28; Matthew 13:1–9, Matthew 13:18–23).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This summary highlights the main theme of the section (Matthew 4:23–9:38): the work and message of the Messiah. In ancient writings, chapters did not exist. Authors would start and end a section with the same phrase (called an inclusio; see Matthew 9:35).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• During the time of Jesus, much of Palestine was under Roman control as part of Syria. At that time, Syria could mean the whole eastern Mediterranean coast. Matthew mentions Syria to show how far news of Jesus spread.

• those having seizures: This refers to epilepsy or demonic possession. In Matthew 17:15, a person described this way "falls into the fire for into the water," meaning the boy could not control himself.

• The Decapolis was a group of ten cities, mostly east of the Jordan River and southeast of the Sea of Galilee. These included: 

• Damascus, 

• Raphana, 

• Hippos, 

• Abila (or Canatha), 

• Gadara, 

• Scythopolis, 

• Pella, 

• Dion, 

• Gerasa, and 

• Philadelphia (Amman). 

These cities were mostly Gentile (non-Jewish) and followed Greek culture.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This is the first of five long teachings in Matthew (see also Matthew 9:35–11:1; Matthew 13:1–53; Matthew 18:1–19:2; Matthew 23:1–26:1). The Sermon on the Mount focuses on the Messiah's call for people to become righteousness. Paul considered righteousness to be God's saving actions and a person's status before God. Jesus uses the term to mean moral behavior that obeys God's will, like the apostle James. Righteousness means doing God's will as Jesus reveals it. This "revelation of righteousness" connects the whole sermon.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
The poor in spirit (compare Luke 6:20, Luke 6:24): in the Old Testament, the poor are often shown as very devoted to God because the rich oppress them. This oppression leads them to trust in the Lord for salvation and help, instead of relying on wealth (Matthew 11:5; Psalms 37:14–15; Psalms 40:17; Psalms 69:28–33; Isaiah 61:1; Isaiah 66:2). 

In both Matthew’s and Luke’s writings, the “poor” are indeed financially poor, but their trust in God, not their poverty, makes them blessed (Isaiah 57:15; Isaiah 66:2).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Those who mourn are the people who felt sad about Israel's spiritual and national condition (see Matthew 23:37–39; Isaiah 61:2–3; Joel 1:8–13; Joel 2:12–13, Joel 2:18–19; Romans 9:1–5; 1 Corinthians 5:2; James 4:9). It may also include to personal sorrow, whether from sin or tragedy (Mark 16:10; Revelation 18:11, Revelation 18:19).

• will be comforted: The passive voice shows respect for God's holy name. It could also mean God will comfort them (see also Matthew 5:6–7, Matthew 5:9). Comfort will come when God fulfills all his promises (Isaiah 40:1–2; Isaiah 61:2–3).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• the meek: Jesus almost directly quotes Psalm 37:11 here. In other places, Jesus describes himself in a similar way, contrasting with other teachers (Matthew 11:29). He also avoids pride (Matthew 12:17–21; Matthew 21:5). Jesus shows this trait through his death on the cross (1 Peter 2:23; 1 Peter 3:9).

• The whole earth could also mean the land, referring to God's promise of land to Abraham and his descendants (Genesis 12:7; Genesis 17:8; see Isaiah 60:21). It might also mean God's rule over the entire earth (Matthew 19:28; Matthew 28:18–20; Psalm 115:16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness: These are either followers of Jesus whose main purpose in life is to obey him (see Matthew 3:15; Matthew 5:10, Matthew 5:20), or they could be people who want justice for everyone (Psalms 11:7; Psalms 85:10–12; Isaiah 11:1–4; Jeremiah 23:5–6; Jeremiah 33:16). They often pray, “Your will be done, on earth” (Matthew 6:10).

• Christ has brought justice and righteousness (Romans 3:21–22; Romans 5:1), and his followers will find satisfaction in it (compare Psalms 42:1–2; Psalms 63:1–2).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus emphasized the great importance of being merciful. This means to show kindness to those in need (see Matthew 6:12, Matthew 6:14–15; Matthew 9:13; Matthew 12:7; Matthew 18:23–35; Matthew 23:23; Matthew 25:31–46). Those who are merciful now will receive God's mercy at the final judgment.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The pure in heart (see Psalms 24:3–5; Psalms 51:7; Isaiah 6:5) differ from those who believed they could please God by following human traditions (see Matthew 23:25–26). Jesus emphasized simple, genuine righteousness from within (see Matthew 6:1–24; Matthew 15:1–20; Matthew 23:23–28; Deuteronomy 6:5).

• They will see God and achieve more than Moses did (see Exodus 33:18–23; Exodus 34:5–7; see also Psalm 73:1).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• This teaching likely addressed zealots. These were Jewish revolutionaries who wanted to overthrow Roman rule with violence. The Messiah’s kingdom would come through different methods.

• the peacemakers: Jesus was not calling for complete pacifism. Instead, he called for a new kind of action.

• Peace means no hostility and the presence of God’s salvation (Leviticus 26:6; 1 Samuel 16:4–5; Isaiah 9:5–6; Zechariah 8:16; Ephesians 2:14; Colossians 1:20). Those who follow Jesus should work for justice, righteousness, reconciliation, and mercy. These should be the effects of God’s salvation through Christ (Matthew 5:43–47; Luke 10:5–6).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The first followers of Jesus were persecuted by Jewish leaders who were offended by the new teaching of Jesus, which revealed God’s truth with authority (see Matthew 10:17–23; Matthew 11:2–6; Matthew 12:1–8; Matthew 15:1–20; Matthew 23:34–36). Since then, following Jesus and his teachings has often led to persecution (Matthew 10:24–25; 2 Timothy 3:12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The great … reward Jesus talks about is not earned by suffering for doing right. It is God's blessing for those who show his grace to others (see Matthew 10:41–42; Matthew 20:1–16). 

• The ancient prophets are closely connected with the New Testament apostles (see also Matthew 13:16–17; Matthew 23:29–36; Ephesians 2:20).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• People used salt for a number of reasons:

• to clean and prevent decay (Ezekiel 16:4), 

• in making agreements (Leviticus 2:13; Numbers 18:19; see study note on 2 Chronicles 13:5), and

• to flavor food (Job 6:6; Mark 9:50).

• Salt that loses its savor becomes useless or tasteless (see Mark 9:50; Luke 14:34).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The good actions of the disciples will positively impact the world, bringing glory to God. Jesus warns them not to do anything that could harm this positive influence.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Light of the world … city on a hill: How the disciples live will inspire others to live the same way and honor God (see Isaiah 2:2–5; Isaiah 42:6; Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 51:4; Isaiah 56:6–8; Isaiah 60:1–3; Philippians 2:15).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Glorify your Father in heaven: Those who pretend to be religious want people to praise them, but the disciples of Jesus should want people to praise God (see 1 Peter 2:12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• To abolish would mean to remove and replace the Law of Moses and the writings of the prophets (that is, the whole Old Testament) as God’s revelation of his will.

• until everything is accomplished: This could mean to obey the Old Testament perfectly, complete their teachings, or fulfill their prophecies (see Matthew 1:22; Matthew 2:15, Matthew 2:17, Matthew 2:23). Jesus himself embodies everything the Prophets and the Law taught and expected. Now that Christ has arrived, who fulfills these writings, we must understand the Old Testament in relation to him (Luke 24:26, Luke 24:44).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The fulfillment of the Law in Christ means that his disciples must obey all of his commands (see Matthew 28:20). 

• commandments: This refers to Old Testament commands (Matthew 5:18) now fulfilled in Christ's teachings (see Matthew 5:21–48).

• least in the kingdom of heaven: Jesus may mean that such a person will still enter the kingdom, but only barely and with low status. Another view, based on some Jewish evidence, is that he means eternal exclusion or damnation (compare Matthew 8:12, where “those for whom the Kingdom was prepared” are shut out forever).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
Unless your righteousness exceeds: The disciples of Jesus need a new kind of righteousness that only he teaches and makes possible. Matthew 5:21–47 shows this and Matthew 5:48 summarizes what it is. 

This righteousness is different in amount and quality. Jesus is greater than the temple (Matthew 12:6) and Jonah (Matthew 12:41). So, the righteousness of his disciples must greatly surpass that of the Jewish religious teachers and Pharisees (see Matthew 3:7–9).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: it was said to the ancients: The expression refers to the traditional interpretation of the teachers of religious law and Pharisees. Their traditions did not allow murder, but they did allow hatred. The righteous way of life required by Jesus surpasses this attitude. It demands people to live in peace with each other (Matthew 5:23–24). It is not enough to only avoid committing murder (Matthew 5:22).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: You have heard … But I tell you: Jesus contrasts his teachings to six misunderstandings of the law. Each example shows the surpassing righteousness of Jesus. Jesus reveals God's will, which contrasts with human traditions.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Judgment … Sanhedrin … hell: The second and third punishments are more severe than usual in the time of Jesus. This emphasizes the surpassing righteousness of Jesus and his followers (see Matthew 5:20). They did not accept unresolved conflicts or treating other people as unimportant. 

• anyone who says to his brother, ‘Raca’: The Aramaic term reqa’ (transliterated as raca) means something like "empty head." This probably means the same thing as cursing someone (literally if you say, ‘You fool’; compare James 2:20). Thinking that other people are unimportant is a sin that expresses itself in different ways.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus provides two examples of making peace in communities and society.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The righteousness of Jesus exposes sin beyond only outward actions. He shows the true purpose of the law.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
Hell (Greek Gehenna): Gehenna was the name of a valley outside Jerusalem. Some kings of Judah used this place to worship idols and even offered children as sacrifices by fire (2 Chronicles 28:3; 2 Chronicles 33:6; Jeremiah 7:31; Jeremiah 32:35). King Josiah eventually destroyed this site (2 Kings 23:10). 

In the New Testament, Gehenna refers to the place where God punishes. Jesus taught that unless his followers live with greater righteousness (living in the right way before God), they will not enter God’s kingdom (Matthew 5:20). Instead, they will face eternal punishment (Matthew 5:22; Matthew 23:33).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: If your right eye causes you to sin, gouge it out and throw it away: These vivid images demand a complete rejection of sin. But even extreme actions like self-harm cannot stop a lustful mind. Jesus calls for a greater righteousness that only he can provide.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: A certificate of divorce is a document that makes a divorce legal. Evidence shows this document allowed remarriage. “The essential formula in the notice of divorce is, ‘Lo, you are free to marry any man.’ … The essential formula in a writ of emancipation is, ‘Lo, you are a freedwoman: lo, you belong to yourself’” (Mishnah Gittin 9:3).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus challenges how people misuse the Old Testament rules about divorce (see Deuteronomy 24:1–4; compare Matthew 19:3–9). Only following the rules does not make divorce right. Jesus permits divorce only for sexual infidelity and bans casual divorce (see also 1 Corinthians 7:10–11).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The exception clause allows, but does not require divorce if a spouse is unfaithful (see also Matthew 19:9). Importantly, Jesus does not require death for the guilty person (see Deuteronomy 22:21–22).

• The idea is that if a man divorces his wife for the wrong reasons, he forces her into adultery by making her remarry. This would violate the law.

• he who marries a divorced woman: It is unclear if Jesus means any divorced woman or only those divorced without a valid reason (like unfaithfulness). Jewish divorce law assumed that legitimate divorces allowed remarriage.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
Jesus explains the Old Testament's teachings on oaths (Leviticus 19:12; Numbers 30:2–4; Deuteronomy 23:21–23; Psalm 50:14; Zechariah 8:17). 

The Pharisees had different levels of commitment for oaths. For example, oaths not mentioning God were less serious. Jesus teaches that everything connects to God. This includes heaven, earth, Jerusalem, my head (see also Matthew 23:16–22). So, breaking any oath disobeys God's command (see Exodus 20:7). 

The main idea is to always be truthful. The teachings of Jesus make a disciple's simple "yes or no" as serious as an oath. Honest people do not need oaths (James 5:12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
The Old Testament allowed fair retribution (payback) (Exodus 21:24–25; Deuteronomy 19:16–21) to keep punishments from being too severe. Yet, Jesus does not allow personal revenge for his disciples. Instead, Jesus teaches finding victory through suffering and the cross (1 Peter 2:23). 

Some consider this teaching as a guide for all aspects of life, including politics. Others consider it to apply to personal willingness to give up rights and forgive as God forgives (see Matt 5:48; Matthew 18:23–35). Like the servant in Isaiah 50:4–9 and Isaiah 53:7 (see also Matthew 12:15–21), the followers of Jesus should apply this virtue to honor, possessions, time, or property. True righteousness does not demand its own way.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Forced labor was a humiliating part of Roman rule (see Matthew 27:32). Jesus transformed it into a chance to joyfully serve God. This saying shows that Jesus opposed Jewish revolutionaries, who called for violent resistance (see Matthew 5:9).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: See Deuteronomy 15:7–11.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Hate your enemy: Jesus is not rejecting the Old Testament. Instead, he is correcting a traditional interpretation that was mistaken (see Exodus 23:4–5). The Old Testament never commands people to “hate your enemy.” The closest verses are in Psalm 139:21–22, where hatred is expressed toward God’s enemies.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: By loving everyone, the followers of Jesus would not become children of God. Their actions would demonstrate that they are already God's true children, living according to his nature and will (see Deuteronomy 10:18–19).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: If you greet only your brothers: Jews were taught to greet Gentiles (non-Jews) to keep peaceful relations. But such greetings were not the same as those given to “brothers,” meaning fellow Jews.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• This verse connects Matthew 5:20–48 as a single unit (see study note on Matthew 4:23–25).

• be perfect: The word “perfect” means maturity, wholeness, and full devotion to God. It describes a complete response to the message of Jesus about the kingdom (Matthew 19:21; Ephesians 4:13; Philippians 3:15; Colossians 1:28; Colossians 4:12; 1 John 4:18). True perfection has love at its center (see Luke 6:36).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• This verse begins the teaching in Matthew 6:2–18. Jesus explains that righteousness (living in line with God’s will) should not be done for public recognition. It should be offered as service to God.

• Righteous acts are actions that follow God’s way of living. Examples include:

• giving gifts to those in need (Matthew 6:2–4), 

• praying (Matthew 6:5–15), and 

• fasting (Matthew 6:16–18). 

Jesus encourages keeping these actions private to avoid seeking personal praise instead of honoring God (compare Matthew 5:16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The hypocrites: see study note on Matthew 23:13. 

• a trumpet: they would blow these during important ceremonies, like times of public fasts.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Your Father … will reward you: This is true both now and at the final judgment, which is at the end of history (see Matthew 25:31–46).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: When you pray: Jews prayed regularly at 9 am and 3 pm (see Acts 3:1). They often gathered for public prayer. Hypocrites purposely chose public places at these times so everyone would notice them.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Go into your inner room: Jesus is not opposed to group prayer (see Matthew 18:19–20; Luke 11:2–4). He tells his disciples not to use prayer to seek attention.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: God cannot be persuaded by repeating words over and over. The Lord’s Prayer is a simple and authoritative model (Matthew 6:9–13), unlike the lengthy prayers of pagans.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• This is how you should pray: This introduces what is often called the Lord’s Prayer. Unlike the long and repeated prayers of pagan worshipers (Matthew 6:7–8).

• Most Jewish prayers did not call God “Father.” But Jesus did so in nearly every prayer. The only exception is his cry on the cross (Mark 15:34). 

• hallowed be Your name: This means that God’s name should be honored. In the Old Testament, God’s name was dishonored when his people sinned (Isaiah 29:22–24; Jeremiah 34:15–16; Ezekiel 39:7; Amos 2:7).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Lord’s Prayer is similar to a typical Jewish prayer called the qaddish. Jesus taught this prayer to his disciples as a brief summary of their new faith.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• When the disciples of Jesus pray for God’s kingdom to come soon, they are asking for his justice, righteousness, peace, and mercy to be established.

• No one rejecting the will of God can enter God's presence (Matthew 7:21; Matthew 12:50; Matthew 21:28–32).

• on earth as it is in heaven: This probably refers to all three petitions, not just the third.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Give us this day our daily bread: A disciple can confidently ask God to provide for daily needs. Then the disciple can continue the work of the kingdom without worry (Matthew 6:25–34).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: As we also have forgiven (see also Matthew 6:14–15; Matthew 18:21–35): Forgiving others shows that a person has repented and received new life from God. This makes our own forgiveness possible. Those who have experienced God’s forgiveness will also forgive. Jesus warns that people who refuse to forgive have not understood God’s mercy and may not have truly repented.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• And lead us not into temptation: Just as Jesus was tested (Matthew 4:1–11), temptation will test a disciple's character. Jesus encourages prayer for God's help to withstand the test (see Matthew 26:41; Psalm 141:4).

• from the evil one: This phrase can also be translated “from evil.” The first reading points to Satan, the one who tempts people (see James 1:13). The second reading points to sin in general. 

• "for Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen": Some later manuscripts add a doxology (a short hymn of praise) at the end of the Lord’s Prayer. It was probably taken from 1 Chronicles 29:11–13 and used to shape the prayer for public worship.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: People often connect prayer and fasting (Leviticus 23:27–32; Nehemiah 9:1–2; Zechariah 7:3–5; Zechariah 8:19; Luke 18:12). Before the time of Jesus, some Israelites misused this practice (Isaiah 58:3–12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Treasures in heaven: For Jews during the time of Jesus, this was a common image. Obeying God’s commands was seen as storing up treasures with God. The context (Matthew 6:19; Luke 12:33) shows that Jesus was mainly referring to acts of charity.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The eye is the lamp: The eye gives light to the body and helps guide the whole person.

• A "good" eye means a morally healthy outlook. It points to simple and wholehearted devotion to God (Matthew 6:24). Here, it also means being generous.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The word translated "money" is traditionally translated mammon. This is an Aramaic term for profits or material possessions. God does not tolerate rivals, so Jesus often warns about the danger of gathering wealth (Matthew 13:22; Matthew 19:16–30; Matthew 26:14–16; Matthew 27:3–10; Matthew 28:11–15). This can become an idol (see Ephesians 5:5; Colossians 3:5). We must trust God to provide our needs (Matthew 4:3–4; Matthew 6:8, Matthew 6:11, Matthew 6:25–34; Matthew 7:7–11; Matthew 10:9–14; Matthew 14:15–21; Matthew 15:32–38). The community of disciples should support each other (Matthew 6:2–4; Matthew 10:40–42; Matthew 19:21; Matthew 23:23–24; Matthew 25:31–46; Matthew 26:6–13; Matthew 27:57–61).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus taught people to live without worry by trusting God to provide for them. His disciples abandoned everything (Matthew 4:18–22; Matthew 9:9; Matthew 10:5–14). Jesus encouraged them that God would provide their needs.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus teaches by moving from lesser to greater: If God the Father cares for the birds (the lesser), he will surely care for his disciples (the greater). Because the disciples are much more valuable to him, they can trust that he will provide for their needs (see also Matthew 10:29–31).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Having little faith comes from not understanding your worth to God and how God's favor protects you.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Gentiles: This word refers to people who do not know God and do not follow his will (see also Matthew 20:19). 

• your heavenly Father knows: Prayer does not give God new information about needs. Prayer shows trust in God to provide what is needed.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Here, Jesus offers a positive alternative to worrying. His disciples should focus on their commitment to God and seek his kingdom through Christ (see Matthew 6:19–24). This should be their main concern.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Mercy is a key theme in the teachings and actions of Jesus (Matthew 9:9–13; Matthew 12:1–7). But Jesus also clearly opposes sin (Matthew 18:15–20; Matthew 23:13–33). Jesus also warns against controlling or condemning others in the name of care. The kind of judgment he forbids is often harsh criticism of small or trivial matters(Matthew 23:23–24). Only God has the right to judge (James 4:11–12).

• do not judge, or you will be judged: This may refer to God's judgment at the end of time (Matthew 5:7). God evaluates us based on how we treat others (Matthew 6:12; Matthew 18:21–35).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus encourages his disciples to serve others instead of condemning them. The contrast of a speck (speck of dust, chip of wood) to a log in the eye is an exaggerated image meant to show the huge difference (see Matthew 5:29; Matthew 23:23–24; compare Micah 6:6–8).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Rabbis often referred to important ideas or Scripture verses as pearls. The mysteries of the kingdom of God (Matthew 13:11) are holy (see Exodus 29:33; Leviticus 2:3; Leviticus 22:10–16; Numbers 18:8–10).

• do not give dogs what is holy: Jews often referred to non-Jewish (Gentile) people as dogs or pigs because these animals were ceremonially unclean (Matthew 15:26; Psalm 22:16, Psalms 22:20; Leviticus 11). Some think this means that many Gentiles would not accept the message of the kingdom. Others see it as a warning about sharing the message of the kingdom with resistant Jewish leaders (see Matthew 5:20; Matthew 10:11–14; see also Hebrews 10:29). It could be a warning to unbelievers in general (see Matthew 18:17; see also 1 Corinthians 2:13–16; 2 Peter 2:21–22).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This passage teaches persistence in prayer. But Jesus does not say God will fulfill extravagant desires. God's people should seek daily needs and spiritual blessings (Matthew 6:10–11).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Law and the Prophets: The teachings of Jesus in Matthew 5:21–7:6 show the true purpose and way to express the law of Moses. Love is central for the disciples of Jesus (see also Galatians 5:13–14, Galatians 5:18).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Enter through the narrow gate: This means deciding to obey Jesus as the Messiah. The wide gate and broad road represent the choice not to follow Jesus or his teachings.

• This path leads to destruction. This means being thrown into fire, being kept out of the kingdom of heaven, being banished from the presence of Jesus, and finally being ruined (Matthew 7:19–23, Matthew 7:27).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Sermon on the Mount ends with a call to decide about Jesus and his teachings (see Matthew 4:23; Matthew 9:35). Those who hear the message of Jesus about the kingdom must obey him to gain eternal life. Or else, they reject him and God will condemn them. There is no third way (Deuteronomy 30:15–20; Psalm 1; Proverbs 12:28; Jeremiah 21:8).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Only a few people accept the truth shown in Christ (see Matthew 19:23; Matthew 20:16; Matthew 22:14; see also John 3:19; John 6:66–71).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
False prophets tell people what they want to hear instead of calling them to obey God's will. Deuteronomy 13:1–5 and Matthew 18:21–22 provide guidelines to determine if someone is a true prophet. A prophet's words must match with God's word, and a prophet's prophecies must come true. 

Jesus explains the first rule. A prophet's actions must match his words to be trustworthy. So, a true prophet's actions will also match God's word. In the same way that fruit shows what kind of tree it comes from, a person's life shows if their inner being is good or not. 

Christians should expect false prophets at the end of time (see Matthew 24:11, Matthew 24:24; Acts 20:28–35; Revelation 13:11–18; Revelation 16:13; Revelation 19:20; Revelation 20:10). Christians can avoid these false prophets misleading them. But Christians must be careful and wise (see 1 Corinthians 12:10; 1 Corinthians 14:29; 1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 4:1–3; Revelation 2:20).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Good fruit and bad fruit symbolize moral behavior (see Matthew 3:8, Matthew 3:10; Matthew 12:33–37; Matthew 13:8; Matthew 21:43; Galatians 5:19–23).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Spiritual rebirth is essential to produce the good actions that Jesus demands. Good works come from faith, and they are inseparable (see James 2:14–26).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The will of My Father: The teachings of Jesus show what the will of the Father is (see also Matthew 12:50; Matthew 21:28–32; Romans 2:13; James 1:22–27).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• On that day: The Old Testament concept behind this idea is the "day of the Lord." On this day, God will save the faithful and condemn those who oppress others (Isaiah 13–14; Joel 2:1–32; Zephaniah 1:14–16). In the teachings of Jesus, this day is when everyone will be judged based on how they respond to him (see Matthew 10:15; Matthew 11:20–24; Matthew 12:36; Matthew 24:19–50; Matthew 25:13, Matthew 25:31–46; Acts 17:31; Romans 2:16).

• Neither spiritual gifts or public accomplishments in the name of Jesus will guarantee God's approval. The decisive issue is obedience (Matthew 7:21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: I never knew you: These people were never truly converted, even though they did great works in the name of God. They refused to follow the Father's will as taught by Jesus, and they continued to break Gods commands. Because they never knew Christ, they never learned to do what he commanded.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• A wise person realizes that Jesus fulfills the Old Testament promises. So a wise person willingly obeys Jesus and chooses to live in such a way that leads to blessings (Matthew 5:3–12; Matthew 7:13–14).

• built his house on the rock: Building a house directly on rock provides a much stronger foundation than would a dry, sandy riverbed or floodplain (Matthew 7:26).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This entire sermon (Matthew 5:3–7:27) focuses on following the teachings of Jesus by living righteously (Matthew 5:20). Listening without obedience is like choosing the wide gate and broad way that leads to ruin (James 1:22–25; James 2:14–26). A decision is necessary in light of what God has revealed (see Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28, Deuteronomy 30:30).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The storm symbolizes God's all-knowing judgment (see Jeremiah 23:19; Ezekiel 1:4).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• At first, Jesus began teaching only his disciples (Matthew 5:1). But large crowds soon followed him up the mountainside.

• The teachers of religious law based their authority on Scripture they quoted or on the traditions of earlier scholars. In contrast, Jesus taught with direct authority.

He did quote Scripture in the Sermon on the Mount. Yet his words carried the weight of his own authority as the Messiah (God’s chosen one).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
Here, the kingdom of God appears with supernatural power (see Matthew 4:23–25; Matthew 11:2–6). It reaches people who were previously excluded from God's blessings. This included: 

• non-Jewish people, 

• lepers, 

• blind people, 

• sick women, 

• people possessed by demons, 

• tax collectors, 

• those with long-term bleeding, and 

• the dead. 

Jesus showed compassion to people in need. But the religious leaders reacted with anger and opposition. Jesus called his followers to respond with faith and to walk in discipleship (living as his learners and followers).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Leprosy refers to various skin diseases. People with leprosy (lepers) were ceremonially unclean and excluded from society. They could only return once they had no symptoms and a priest declared them clean (see Matthew 8:4; Leviticus 14:2–32). Sometimes leprosy was a judgment from God (Numbers 12:9–15; 2 Kings 5:27; 2 Kings 15:5).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Be clean: When Jesus healed lepers, it showed the presence of God's kingdom in him and his work (Matthew 11:2–6).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The healed leper would show everyone that the religious leaders were wrong not to trust the Messiah (Matthew 10:18) or that Jesus followed the law of Moses (Matthew 5:17).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Capernaum is on the Sea of Galilee, four kilometers (about two and a half miles) west of where the Jordan River flows out. In the time of Jesus, it was a thriving fishing village. Located at an important crossroads on the Great Trunk Road, it connected Mesopotamia and Egypt. It was an international village. Much of the ministry Jesus did in Galilee happened there (for example, Matthew 4:13; Matthew 8:14–17).

• The centurion: He was one of sixty commanders in a legion and led 100 Roman soldiers (see also Mark 15:39; Acts 10:1; Acts 27:1).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus once again served people who were pushed aside or rejected. The centurion was a Gentile soldier. Helping him would have caused strong anger from both nationalistic Jews and separatist Jews.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: I will go (compare Acts 10:9–35; Galatians 2:11–14): Some scholars interpret this as a question: Should I [a Jew] enter [a Gentile's house, risking impurity] and heal him?

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The centurion recognized the authority of Jesus. From his own experience, he knew his soldiers quickly obeyed his orders. He realized that God had given Jesus the authority to perform miracles. The centurion’s faith demonstrates that the kingdom of God includes people from all nations (Matthew 8:11).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The coming of Gentiles fulfills Old Testament promises (Isaiah 2:2–3). God promised Abraham that he would be a blessing to many nations, not just the Jewish people (Genesis 18:18). Christ fulfills this promise (Galatians 3:8, Galatians 3:16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: with a word: Jesus showed his powerful authority. His words alone could heal and give life.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus has authority to heal every disease and rule over every demon.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases: When he took on the sins of humanity, the Messiah also carried our sickness (infirmities and diseases). Diseases exist because sin is in the world. One effect of Jesus taking our sin on the cross is physical healing (1 Peter 2:24). When Jesus healed people and cast out evil spirits, he showed that he is the Messiah (God's chosen one) as Scripture promised (see Matthew 11:2–6; Matthew 12:28; 1 Corinthians 11:29–30; James 5:13–16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus once met two people who said they wanted to be his followers. Jesus explained what it really means to follow him. He wanted them to understand that following him required serious commitment.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The teachers of religious law had an honored job. They preserved, learned, and explained the Scriptures to benefit society. People thought the way to God was through them (Matthew 15:13–14; Matthew 23:13).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Being a disciple of Jesus is not easy. It requires more than knowing the right things. Following Jesus includes being willing to give up life’s normal comforts.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Another of His disciples: This statement suggests that the teacher in verse Matthew 8:19 was also a disciple. Calling Jesus "Lord" shows a strong commitment to him.

• bury my father: In Judaism, this was a very important religious duty. But Jesus requires complete dedication to him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Let the dead bury their own dead. Those who opposed Jesus might have seen these words as ignoring the commandment to honor parents (Exodus 20:12). But it actually reinforces the first commandment (Exodus 20:1–3). The authority of Jesus as the Messiah justified this statement. Living for the kingdom of heaven influences normal human life, including family ties and commitments (see Matthew 10:34–39; Matthew 12:46–50; Matthew 19:29; Zechariah 13:3; Luke 14:26–27).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This story continues the theme of true discipleship. In the storm, the disciples had to trust Jesus with their very lives for safety and rescue. Jesus showed that he even has authority over dangerous weather and the sea (see Job 38:8–11; Psalms 29; Psalms 65:1–13; Psalms 89:9; Psalms 107:23–32).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: A fierce storm came upon the lake. Sudden strong winds are common on the Sea of Galilee since mountains surround it.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: What kind of man is this?: To receive salvation, people must recognize who Jesus is and put their trust in him. At this point, his disciples still did not understand.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
demon-possessed … so violent: When people were possessed by demons, they often became violent. Other signs included:

• fear of the Son of God (Matthew 8:29), 

• being unable to speak (Matthew 9:32; Matthew 12:22), 

• blindness (Matthew 12:22), 

• seizures (Matthew 17:15), 

• and doing things to hurt themselves (Matthew 17:15). 

When Jesus cast out demons, it showed that the power of God’s kingdom had entered human history (Matthew 12:28).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This event focuses on the authorityof Jesus and the cost of being his disciple. Those who have faith, like the Messiah, will experience opposition.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Those controlled by Satan immediately recognized Jesus as the Son of God (see Mark 1:24). This answered the question asked by the disciples of Jesus when he calmed the storm (Matthew 8:27). In other places, the true nature and identity of Jesus are acknowledged by the Father (Matthew 3:17; Matthew 17:5), Satan (Matthew 4:3, Matthew 4:6), people (Matthew 14:33; Matthew 16:16; Matthew 27:54), and Christ himself (Matthew 11:27; Matthew 24:36; Matthew 28:19).

• the appointed time: This phrase points to the final judgment. At that time, God will condemn forever all who oppose him (see Jude 1:6; Revelation 20:10).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The demons could not resist the power of Jesus. They begged to escape their coming destruction.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The words of Jesus had power to drive out demons.

• died in the waters: This showed that Jesus had begun to defeat the enemy (Matthew 12:28; Luke 10:17–20; Romans 16:20; Colossians 2:15).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The sad part is that people who saw the Son of God's power to save were afraid of change, so they rejected him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus lived in Capernaum (Mark 2:1). He seems to have moved there from Nazareth after the people of Nazareth rejected him (Matthew 4:13; Luke 4:16–31).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: There was debate and conflict among Jesus opponents. This included the teachers of the law and the Pharisees (Matthew 9:1–13), and also the disciples of John the Baptist (Matthew 9:14–17).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This man is blaspheming: Only God can forgive sins (Psalm 103:3; Isaiah 43:25; Jeremiah 50:20). The teachers of religious law failed to understand the mission of Jesus as God's Son who became human (Matthew 3:17; Matthew 11:25–27). As God's Messiah (Matthew 1:1; Matthew 11:2–6), Jesus was saving humanity (Matthew 8:17; Matthew 26:26–28).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: It may seem easier for Jesus to say, “Your sins are forgiven,” since no one can see immediate proof. But it is much harder to heal a paralyzed man so that he can walk. The visible miracle proved that Jesus had the authority to forgive sins. It forced those who saw it to decide what they believed about him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: So that you may know: Jesus performed the miracle to demonstrate his authority and identity as God's Messiah (see Matthew 11:2–6; Matthew 12:28).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The crowd responded with fear and admiration because they realized a powerful truth about Jesus. He is truly the Son of God with the authority to forgive sins on earth (Matthew 9:6).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Another name for the apostle Matthew was Levi (Mark 2:14). He might have had two names, or Jesus might have given him a new name.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus, as Lord and Messiah, removed the obstacles that stopped righteous Jews from interacting with people considered ceremonially unclean or sinful.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
The Jewish people hated Jewish tax collectors (Matthew 5:46–47; Matthew 18:15–20). This was because they worked with Roman rulers. Jews considered them traitors against Israel. Many also considered them ceremonially unclean because of their contact with Gentiles and the images on Roman coins. 

Tax collection was a private business. In each area, Rome gave the right to collect taxes to the highest bidder (compare Luke 19:1–10). Collectors kept any money they gathered above their bid. Out of greed, they often used threats to get the money.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• I desire mercy, not sacrifice: Jesus applies this desire of God to eating with sinners. Jesus showed mercy by eating with them. This contrasted with the Pharisees who avoided sinners. They considered their avoidance to symbolize sacrifices. 

• Jesus exposed the Pharisees' true spiritual state. The Pharisees considered themselves to be righteous. But they were actually unrighteous and needed the Messiah to save them (Matthew 7:1–5; Matthew 8:11–12; Matthew 19:30; Matthew 20:16; Matthew 21:43).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
Fast: Fasting was a way to show humility and repentance before God (2 Samuel 12:16–23; Daniel 9:3). It also reminded the nation of their need to repent (Leviticus 16:29–31; Nehemiah 9:1). Some believed fasting would help bring the Messiah more quickly by purifying God’s people.

Jesus and his disciples did not fast (Matthew 11:18–19) This was a quiet but clear message: the Messiah had already come (see also Matthew 6:16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The guests of the bridegroom: John the Baptist described the Messiah and his disciples this way (John 3:29). He used Old Testament images to show who Jesus really was (see Matthew 25:1–13; Isaiah 54:5–6).

• taken away: This is the first prediction Jesus made about his violent death (see Matthew 16:21; Matthew 17:12, Matthew 17:22–23; Matthew 20:18–19; Matthew 26:2, Matthew 26:26–35; Isaiah 53:8).

• then they will fast: Jesus might be talking about the disciples' sadness right after his crucifixion, or their way of living after his death and resurrection (see Acts 9:9; Acts 13:2–3; Acts 14:23; Acts 27:9, Acts 27:33).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: These short parables compare the new covenant (the promises between God and his people) that Jesus began (Matthew 6:26–29) with the old covenant. The comparison focuses especially on religious ceremonies like fasting. Jesus completes the law, but he does not cancel it (Matthew 5:17–20; see Galatians 2:21; Galatians 5:4). At the same time, the new covenant brings new practices.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Place Your hand on her: Placing hands on someone is a visible sign of praying for God's power to help them. It often results in new life or ministries (Matthew 19:13; Numbers 27:18–23; Deuteronomy 34:9).

• The man believed Jesus could raise the dead (see 1 Kings 17:8–24; 2 Kings 4:18–37).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus is the Messiah with limitless power. He invites people to trust in him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Because of her constant bleeding, the woman was always considered ceremonially unclean. Anyone she touched was also unclean (Leviticus 15:25–30). But when she touched Jesus, instead of making him unclean, she was made clean. This surprising reversal shows the power to heal, redeem, and make holy (see Matthew 14:36; Mark 3:10). 

• fringe: The tassels at the bottom of a tunic (Matthew 23:5; Numbers 15:37–41) reminded Jews to obey God's law.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Your faith has healed you (literally has saved you): Her physical healing showed her spiritual salvation (see Matthew 8:17).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: the flute players and the noisy crowd: people publicly expressed their sorrow over a family member's death. This happened with music and laments by professional mourners. “Even the poorest in Israel should hire at least two flutes and one wailing woman” (Mishnah Ketubbot 4:4).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The girl had died, but Jesus said she was only asleep. He meant that she would soon be raised to life again (see Isaiah 26:19; John 11:11–14, John 11:25; 1 Thessalonians 4:14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Eye diseases were common in ancient times. People often considered blindness as divine punishment (see Exodus 4:11; Deuteronomy 28:28; 2 Kings 6:18; John 9:2–3). The Old Testament prophesies that when the Messiah came he would restore sight to the blind (Matthew 11:4–5; Isaiah 29:18–19; Isaiah 35:5–6). 

• Son of David is a title connected to the Messiah and miraculous healings (see Matthew 1:1; Matthew 12:23; Matthew 15:22; Matthew 20:30–31; 2 Samuel 7:12–16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus asked the question to encourage the two men to express their faith in him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Healing the deaf so that they can hear, and the mute so that they can speak, is a sign of the kingdom of God (Matthew 11:4–5; Isaiah 35:5–6).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Messiah's actions inspire faith, surprise, and sometimes mocking rejection.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This verse links to the section that started in Matthew 4:23. Matthew has shown Jesus as the Messiah who teaches, preaches, heals, and expels demons. Jesus calls the people to make a decision to trust in him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus expands his ministry (see Matthew 4:23–9:34) by sending his disciples to other people in Israel (Matthew 10:5–6). The instructions Jesus gives his disciples (Matthew 10:5–42) emphasizes missionary work and the opposition and challenges they will encounter.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Like sheep without a shepherd: Jesus grieved the failure of the Pharisees to guide the people with care (see Matthew 12:11–12; Matthew 18:12). Their constant attacks against him showed their hard-hearted rejection of God. Because of this neglect and mistreatment, the crowds suffered greatly (Matthew 10:5–6; Matthew 15:12–14; Matthew 23:4; Zechariah 11:16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Harvest refers to the great number of people who are ready to hear and respond to God’s message (see also Matthew 13:24–30, Matthew 13:36–43; Mark 4:26–29; John 4:35–38; Revelation 14:15–20). 

• the Lord of the harvest: God is the true master of the harvest. All ministries are under his call (see Matthew 23:8–10, Matthew 23:13). So Jesus encourages his disciples to pray for God to send out more workers.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Jesus called his twelve disciples as workers in the harvest (Matthew 9:37–38). Choosing twelve was on purpose, reminding people of the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus was appointing new leaders for God's new people under his rule as the Messiah (Matthew 16:18–19; Matthew 18:18; Matthew 19:28; Matthew 21:43). 

• Jesus gave them authority (Matthew 9:6–8; Matthew 28:18): Jesus empowered the twelve apostles to perform tasks that Jewish leaders could not do (Matthew 9:32–34; Matthew 10:5–8). Jesus shows his authority to cast out evil spirits (Matthew 8:28) and to heal in similar ways (Matthew 4:23; Matthew 8:1–9:35).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The apostles are ambassadors sent by Christ's authority to represent him and complete specific tasks (see Matthew 10:1–8, Matthew 10:40; Matthew 28:16–20). The term apostle also refers to Paul (Galatians 1:1). 

• first Simon, called Peter: Peter was the first apostle chosen by Jesus (Matthew 4:18–22; Matthew 16:17–19). He served as the leader of the apostles (see Matthew 19:27; Matthew 26:33; Acts 2:14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
The New Testament contains four lists of the apostles (see also Mark 3:16–19; Luke 6:14–16; Acts 1:13). These lists are slightly different.

The order of names changes, but the groups remain the same. The main difference is between “Thaddaeus” (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18) and “Judas son of James” (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13). These may be two names for the same person.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Matthew, the tax collector (see Matthew 9:9), is also known as Levi (Mark 2:14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• the Zealot: Zealots were militant Jews who believed violence and war could achieve God's will. As a Jewish nationalist, Simon was probably passionate about the law (Acts 22:3–5; Galatians 1:14; Philippians 3:6). The Jewish historian Josephus blamed the Zealot party for the major war with Rome from AD 66–70. 

• Iscariot might refer to someone from Kerioth in southern Judea (Joshua 15:25) or from Kerioth in Perea (Jeremiah 48:24).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles: At this time, the mission of Jesus was limited to the Jews (Matthew 15:24). God would reach Gentiles (non-Jewish people) through the Jews (Isaiah 2:2–4; Isaiah 42:6–7; Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 60:3). 

• Jews saw Samaritans as impure Jews (Luke 17:18) because they married gentiles during and after the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles (2 Kings 17:24–41). The tension between Jews and Samaritans grew worse in 128 BC when John Hyrcanus, a Jewish leader, destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim (Josephus, Antiquities 13.9.1).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: They are lost because their shepherds (leaders) neglected them (Matthew 9:36; Matthew 15:24).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: By doing these things in the name and authority of Jesus, the apostles showed that Jesus is the Messiah (see Matthew 11:2–6).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Freely you have received; freely give: While payment is not wrong (1 Corinthians 9:3–19; Galatians 6:6; 1 Timothy 5:17), Jesus encouraged the apostles to avoid appearing greedy (see Acts 8:20; Acts 20:33).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus' disciples should trust God to provide (Matthew 6:11, Matthew 6:25–34; Matthew 7:7–11). They should avoid greed, which could harm God's reputation. They should also encourage new communities to provide what their leaders need (see 1 Corinthians 9:3–19).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: greet its occupants: Greetings meant more than just saying "hello." They often included a blessing for the person receiving it (see Ruth 2:4).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• A worthy home would accept the message about Jesus and the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 10:37–38; Matthew 22:8). 

• The disciples’ blessing was an offer of salvation. Taking back the blessing was a sign of judgment as the offer was removed.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
Shake the dust off your feet: This act was like the actions of a prophet. It came from an Israelite custom: when crossing back into Israel, they would shake off the dust of Gentile lands to show rejection of ungodliness.

For the disciples, the gesture meant rejecting those who opposed God’s work (see Acts 18:6). Speaking judgment on those who refuse the message was part of proclaiming the good news about God’s kingdom (see Matthew 11:20–24; Matthew 13:10–15; Matthew 23:37–39; Matthew 24:1–36).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah because of their evil actions (Genesis 18:16–19:29). With the fuller revelation through Jesus Christ, a town that rejected the disciples' message would receive a more severe judgment. 

• that town: A whole village or city is responsible when most people reject the message (see Acts 13:45–47, Acts 13:50–51; Acts 14:1–7). But God will save individuals who trust in him (for example, Lot; see Genesis 19:1–29; 2 Peter 2:6–9).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Scripture often compares false leaders who exploit people’s spiritual weakness, instead of giving proper care, to wolves (Ezekiel 22:27; Zephaniah 3:3; compare Proverbs 28:15). 

• be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves: This proverb means to be wise and careful, but not deceitful or violent.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Just as God gave Moses a spokesman in Aaron (Exodus 4:10–17), God would also give Jesus disciples the right words at the right time through the Spirit (John 14:26; Acts 4:8).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Jewish people often connected family conflict with the end times (see Matthew 24:9–10). Jesus himself went through such conflict (Matthew 12:46–50). 

• The one who perseveres to the end means those who stay loyal to Jesus, even to death or until he returns (Matthew 10:23). 

• will be saved: Some interpret this as being freed from persecution, like release from prison. But here it refers to eternal salvation for those who stay faithful.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• before the Son of Man comes: Scholars disagree on whether this refers to Christ's second coming for his church or an earlier judgment, specifically the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (see Matthew 16:28). 

• you will not reach: Jesus might mean “before you have fled through all the towns” or “before you have spread the gospel in all the towns.” The focus on persecution in the context (see Matthew 10:17–39) supports the first idea. It suggests the towns were like cities of refuge (Numbers 35:9–32). This emphasizes how widely they will reject the message. It means “not until the whole nation has expelled you.”

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: In the time of Jesus, people often called Satan "the prince of demons." The Greek word used is Beelzeboul, which comes from the name of an Old Testament pagan god, Baal-zebul (“lord, the prince”). In the Latin Bible, the name appears as Beelzebub. This form reflects a Hebrew phrase meaning “lord of flies.” It was likely a Jewish insult against Baal-zebul (see 2 Kings 1:2).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The disciples of Jesus should only fear God by obeying him and testifying about him. Unlike human authorities, God's authority and judgment have no limits. 

• hell: See study note on Matthew 5:29.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: God cares for every sparrow. So, the disciples of Jesus, who are more valuable, should not fear. God will take care of them.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: God accepts those who publicly acknowledge Jesus in times of trial and persecution (Matthew 10:16–25). These verses describe a person’s overall way of life, not just a single confession or denial (see Matthew 7:13–27). For example, Judas sometimes acknowledged Jesus but was still condemned (Matthew 26:23–24). Peter denied Jesus (see Matthew 26:69–75), but he was restored and saved.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus did bring peace (John 14:27), but not the kind of social or political peace people often expect. Instead, he called people to make a decision about him. This decision would bring a sword, meaning division, even within families (see Matt 8:21–22; Matthew 12:46–50; Luke 12:51).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Being loyal to Jesus is more important than being loyal to family.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The cross was a tool used by the Romans for torture and execution (Matthew 27:27–55). To take up your cross and follow Jesus means loving him more than anything else. It also means being ready to obey him, no matter the physical or social consequences.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• a prophet’s reward: This can mean either the same reward a prophet gets or the benefits of a prophet's service. 

• a righteous man: This is someone who follows God’s law as taught by John the Baptist (Matthew 21:32) and Jesus (see Matthew 3:15). This is why God approves of them (Matthew 13:43, Matthew 13:49; Matthew 25:37–46).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: One of these little ones: This probably refers to the low social status of most of the disciples of Jesus (see Matthew 5:3; Matthew 18:1–5 and Matthew 6:5; Matthew 23:5–12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Herod Antipas arrested John (Matthew 4:12) because John criticized Herod's immoral relationship with Herodias, the wife of his half-brother (Matthew 14:1–12). 

• the works of Christ: These actions showed that Jesus is the Messiah (Christ) (Matthew 8:1–9:34).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This section starts with John the Baptist’s doubt. It ends by honoring his faith and his work (Matthew 11:7–19). The people's rejection of John (Matthew 11:16–19) hints at their future rejection of Jesus.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This section focuses on two main reactions to Jesus: acceptance and rejection. The first part (Matthew 11:2–12:50) shows Jewish leaders rejecting Jesus, while his disciples are learning to understand and accept him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The miracles of compassion that Jesus did showed that the kingdom of God had begun (see Matthew 12:28; Isaiah 29:18–19; Isaiah 35:5–6; Isaiah 61:1). Jesus expected John to realize he was fulfilling Old Testament prophecies.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Who does not fall away on account of Me: Jesus intended that the works mentioned in verse 5 were meant to help John the Baptist and his disciples decide about Jesus. But Jesus knew that some unexpected parts of his ministry would cause people to reject him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: A reed swaying in the wind: This refers to an unstable person. The implied answer to this rhetorical question is "no."

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: John the Baptist was the greatest person ever to have lived. Yet the least of the followers of Jesus are greater than John because they live in the new covenant of salvation through Jesus (see Matthew 4:17). The new covenant refers to God's new agreement with people that came through Jesus. Salvation (being saved from sin and its consequences) comes through death and resurrection of Jesus.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The kingdom of heaven has been subject to violence: The Greek verb can mean either that the kingdom suffers violence (negative) or that it forcefully advances (positive). In Luke 16:16, a different verb (“preached”) makes the statement clearly positive.
