• the violent lay claim to it: This phrase can also have either a negative or positive sense. Negatively, it may point to those who opposed John (see Matthew 11:2; Matthew 14:1–12) and persecuted the kingdom’s messengers. Positively, it may refer to people “forcing their way in” (see Luke 16:16), urgently pressing into the kingdom through radical trust and obedience.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: He is the Elijah who was to come: John fulfills the Old Testament prophecy about the prophet Elijah's return (Matthew 17:10–13; see Malachi 4:5).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: John’s message was like funeral songs. He lived with strict self-denial, fasting often and not drinking wine (Matthew 11:18; see Matthew 3:4). The message of Jesus is more like wedding songs, with feasting and drinking (see Matthew 9:9–17). In both cases, the people of this time respond to God's messenger with indifference and rejection.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
Here Jesus describes how both John and he himself offended the people of that generation.

John lived in the wilderness, eating locusts and honey (Matthew 3:1, Matthew 3:4). People accused him of having a demon. 

Jesus, by contrast, ate and drank freely with others. People accused him of being like a rebellious son (see Deuteronomy 21:18–21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The miracles Jesus performed showed he was the Messiah (Matthew 11:5–6). These miracles demanded people to repent (Matthew 11:20). Those who rejected the Messiah faced great judgment, because Jesus had clearly shown who he is.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: As Jesus traveled through the villages of Galilee (Korazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum) he revealed more of himself to the people. Because of this greater revelation, their refusal to listen brought a more severe judgment. Jesus compared their judgment to that of the pagan cities Tyre (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26:1–28:19), Sidon (Ezekiel 28:20–23), and Sodom (Genesis 18:22–19:29).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Hades: This is the Greek equivalent to the Hebrew term Sheol (see study note on Psalm 6:5).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The wise and learned: The Pharisees and teachers of religious law thought their access to God was guaranteed through their knowledge and practice of the law. The disciples of Jesus were more childlike (see Matthew 21:15–16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This passage is about the small group of people who accept the Messiah and follow his teachings, even though most of their generation does not.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus showed his close relationship with the Father. Everything he said and did came from his unity with his Father (see John 10:14–15; John 14:6–7; John 15:23–24; John 16:15; John 17:25–26).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The heavy burdens were probably caused by the legal demands of the religious teachers and Pharisees (see Matthew 23:4). 

• rest: This means spiritual refreshment, either now or in the future (compare Matthew 1:21; Hebrews 4:8–11).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
A yoke, which connects two animals, symbolizes the demands of being a disciple of Jesus. Unlike the "yoke" of religious leaders, the yoke of Jesus is easy and light. This is not because it demands less of a person (see Matthew 7:13–14). But it is because the Messiah's power through the Holy Spirit makes it possible (see Acts 15:10; 1 John 5:3). 

Israel's spiritual leaders imposed religious demands (see Matthew 23:4; Acts 15:10). This included 613 Old Testament commands and added traditions. Jesus urged those burdened by the Pharisees' rules to come to him (see Matthew 11:28) to find the salvation for which they deeply longed. This call to salvation involves living obediently to the new teachings of Jesus. Jesus invites people to build a relationship with a humble and gentle teacher.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Sabbath was the seventh day of the week. God intended it to be a day of complete rest according to Old Testament laws (Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:8–11). Christ fulfills the Sabbath (compare Hebrews 4:1–11).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This exchange shows the Pharisees' lack of compassion as they placed a heavy burden on others (Matthew 11:29–30).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Matthew closely connects the offer of rest Jesus gives (Matthew 11:28–30) with a discussion about the Sabbath. The rest Jesus offers liberates people from human traditions about the Sabbath (see Hebrews 4:1–11). The Pharisees rejected Jesus because they had a commitment to their tradition.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Sometimes it was right to suspend ceremonial laws (1 Samuel 21:1–6).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Pharisees did not understand that God designed the Sabbath to benefit people. They made it a heavy burden instead.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Priests worked on the Sabbath (Leviticus 24:8–9; Numbers 28:9–10), and the Pharisees did not find this offensive. If the priests’ work for the temple on the Sabbath is allowed, then certainly Jesus can do the same because he is greater than the temple (see Matthew 4:23; Matthew 9:35; Matthew 11:2–6, Matthew 11:20–30).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Pharisees misunderstood the meaning of the Sabbath. Their view went against Scripture because it ignored the greater principle of mercy.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus is greater than King David, the priests, and the temple. He also rules over the Sabbath.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: their synagogue: A separation was developing between Jesus and Judaism (also Matthew 4:23).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This second Sabbath controversy criticizes the Pharisees for prioritizing rules over people's needs (see Matthew 12:7, Matthew 12:11–12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Is it lawful: Jewish teachers of the law said healing on the Sabbath was allowed only if someone’s life was in danger. Because the person’s life was not in danger, the Pharisees believed that healing was not allowed.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: They rescued animals but ignored people, which was inconsistent.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This summary of the ministry of Jesus explains that Jesus is the Messiah, God's servant who will bring salvation to all nations (see Isaiah 42:1–4).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• This quote is similar to the story of the baptism of Jesus (Matthew 3:13–17). 

• Justice (or judgment): This can be good or bad. Here, it probably means something positive (Matthew 12:20; compare Matthew 23:23).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus does not add to people’s spiritual burdens. Instead, he gives them forgiveness with compassion and the sustenance (nourishment and strength) they need (see Matthew 11:28–30; Matthew 12:1–14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Pharisees, the teachers of religious law, and many people of his generation rejected the Messiah.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• People were amazed by the miracles Jesus performed (Mark 2:12; Mark 6:51; Luke 2:47; Luke 8:56; Luke 24:22). 

• Could this be: The question expected a negative answer. Jesus did not fit their idea of the Messiah, but his miracles made them wonder.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Beelzebul: See study note on Matthew 10:25.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus said in essence, “If I drive out demons by the power of Satan, then Satan is fighting against his own kingdom. That would be foolish for him to do.”

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: your sons: Jesus forced them to think consistently. If Satan's power casts out demons, then the disciples of the Pharisees were just as guilty, since they too cast out demons (see Acts 19:13–16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Pharisees were confronted with the kingdom of God and chose to reject it (see Luke 17:20–21; 1 John 3:8). Through his miracles, Jesus showed the power of the kingdom in the present world. But the kingdom will reach its full completion when Christ comes again.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• This parable forced the Pharisees to answer a simple question. Can anyone drive out demons without first controlling Satan's powers and opposing him (see Isaiah 49:24–26; Isaiah 53:12)? 

• ties up the strong man: This points to how Jesus defeated Satan. He overcame him in the wilderness temptation (Matthew 4:1–11), continued to overcome him throughout his ministry (see Luke 10:17–20), and won the final victory at the cross (see Colossians 2:14–15).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Pharisees accused Jesus of being under the influence of Satan. Jesus explained that he, as the Messiah, cast out demons through the power of the Holy Spirit. In this context, blasphemy against the Holy Spirit can only mean attributing the ministry and exorcisms of Jesus to Satan’s power.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: God can forgive people who are confused about Jesus calling himself the "Son of Man." But, God will not forgive a person that says the Holy Spirit's work comes from Satan. Today, this is like completely rejecting the conviction of the Holy Spirit about Jesus. This refers to when an unbeliever ultimately rejects the good news about Jesus (see Hebrews 6:4–6; 1 John 5:16–21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus addressed the main issue. The Pharisees did not accept him or believe his work came from God because they were wicked (see Matthew 7:15–27).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The careless word, in this context, was the claim that demons empowered Jesus. 

• What a person says will either free or condemn them on the day of judgment. What people say shows the true state of their hearts.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: See a sign: People expected the Messiah to perform amazing miracles. This expectation was probably inspired by stories about Moses (Exodus 4:1–9; see also Isaiah 7:11, Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 38:7–8). They believed the Messiah would show these miracles on demand (see Matthew 16:1–4; Luke 23:8; John 2:18; John 4:48; John 6:30; John 7:31; John 9:16; John 11:47; 1 Corinthians 1:22).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• To demand a sign shows a lack of faith. 

• The sign of the prophet Jonah was his "resurrection" from the large fish after three days and nights. It also referred to his preaching (Matthew 12:41; Luke 11:32). This was similar to the burial, resurrection, and preaching of Jesus. Jesus compared Jonah's experience to what he would experience. He was not predicting the exact timing of his death and resurrection. 

• Heart of the earth is another way of saying "the grave."

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: One greater: Jesus is greater than the temple (Matthew 12:6), the prophet Jonah, and King Solomon. So, rejecting him brings more severe judgment on this "wicked and adulterous generation" (Matthew 12:39).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Queen of the South: see 1 Kings 10:1–13.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: People believed demons liked the dry desert (see Revelation 18:2; compare Isaiah 13:21; Isaiah 34:14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Messiah came in victory over evil spirits. But instead of turning back to God, the nation as a whole rejected him. Jesus said that when an evil spirit is cast out, it may return if the person is not ready to resist it. In the same way, judgment would come on this evil generation because they rejected the Messiah (God’s chosen one).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Those who are true members in the family of Jesus obey the will of God. They show this obedience by obeying the commands of Jesus (see Matthew 7:21). Obedience does not earn entrance into this family, but a person cannot be a member of this family if they do not obey him (see Matthew 3:15; Matthew 5:17–48; Matthew 6:10, Matthew 6:12; Matthew 7:13–27; Matthew 21:31).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: In the third major speech recorded by Matthew (see study note on Matthew 5:1–7:29), Jesus here recognized the separation of his followers from others (Matthew 13:14, Matthew 13:16). He began to reveal the secrets of the kingdom of heaven privately to them through parables.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• This parable (explained in Matthew 13:18–23) discusses the mostly negative reactions of the Jewish people to Jesus and his message. 

• Parables (Greek parabolē): These are stories that use everyday life to explain a spiritual truth. To understand a parable, find the main comparison (analogy) and consider its historical and gospel context. Then a person can understand the main message. Avoid finding unintended symbolic meanings in every part of a parable.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• From this point on, Jesus rarely taught the general public. Instead, he focused on teaching those who had committed themselves to him (Matthew 13:1–20:34). But he would once again confront Israel (Matthew 21:1–23:39). 

• The people were the unbelieving opponents mentioned again in Matthew 13:11 (“them”) and Matthew 13:12 (“whoever does not have”).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The knowledge … has been given to you: God allowed the disciples to understand the importance of Jesus. God also allowed them to respond to the message of Jesus about the kingdom of heaven with faith and obedience (see Matthew 13:19, Matthew 13:23). 

• the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven: Salvation is available through Jesus as the fulfillment of Old Testament promises.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus answered the disciples question in verse 10. He told them that the Jews' stubborn disbelief and rejection of him brought God's condemnation.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Jesus told parables, and those who believed him understood them. Yet, those who rejected Jesus found that his parables increased their disbelief. 

• Though seeing, they do not see … hear or understand: They lacked the faith to recognize the truth (Matthew 13:19, Matthew 13:23) and respond (Mark 8:18; John 12:40; see also Jeremiah 5:21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
Similar to the message of the prophet Isaiah, the message of Jesus has two effects:

• It judges those who do not believe or obey, and 

• it creates a small group of faithful people who do the Lord's will (Matthew 21:43).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus fulfilled what the prophets and Old Testament believers wanted to see and hear. He fulfills the Old Testament promises (see Isaiah 52:15; John 8:56; 1 Peter 1:10).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Does not understand it: Responding to God's message directly relates to understanding its importance.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Has no root, he remains for only a season: The issue is a lack of enduring faith and obedience (see Matthew 7:13–27; Matthew 10:22), especially when confronted by persecution.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus talked about the competing demands in life (see also Matthew 8:18–22). The worries of life can become overwhelming and lead people away from faithful obedience (see Matthew 6:19–34). The temptation of wealth, especially its deceptive nature, is a common theme in Matthew (for example, Matthew 4:8–10; Matthew 6:24; Matthew 13:44–45). God values faith, obedience, and helping those in need more than wealth (for example, Matthew 19:21; Matthew 25:31–46).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Produces a crop: This probably refers to faithfully obeying the commands of Jesus (for example, Matthew 5:1–7:27; Matthew 28:20).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Matthew 13:36–43 explains this story.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Weeds, also known as tares or bearded darnel, look a lot like wheat. Farmers waited until the plants grew to tell them apart. Intentionally contaminating crops like this was against the law.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus rebuked the sons of Zebedee for wanting to destroy villages that did not believe in him (Luke 9:54–55). He told his disciples not to seek revenge against enemies. Judgment is God's responsibility (see Matthew 7:1–5). Jesus urges his disciples to wait patiently for God's righteous judgment ("the harvest"; see Luke 13:6–9).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus used surprising and vivid images in these parables. He probably wanted to show how the kingdom of Heaven would grow through preaching the good news. More probably, he wanted to highlight the contrast between small beginnings and a glorious end. He also encouraged the disciples to be patient (see also Matthew 16:24–17:13).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Usually, yeast refers to the influence of evil (for example, Matthew 16:6; 1 Corinthians 5:6; Galatians 5:9). But in this context it represents the positive and widespread influence of the kingdom of Heaven.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Even the way Jesus taught fulfilled prophecies from the Old Testament. Psalm 78:2–3 talks about sharing the history of God's revelation with future generations. What Jesus revealed in his teachings are the most important part of that history (Matthew 13:10–17; 1 Corinthians 2:7).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• They went into the house (see Matthew 13:1). Jesus taught in public using parables, but he explained their meanings privately to his disciples. 

• Explain: The disciples had the special opportunity to learn the secrets of the kingdom (Matthew 13:11–17). But they did not understand the parables until Jesus explained them.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
These verses explain the parable from Matthew 13:24–30. The people of the kingdom (like wheat) live side by side with those who do not belong to it (like weeds). The “field” is the world, and this will continue until the end of history. 

The mystery of the kingdom is that it is already present in the world, but God has not yet removed the wicked in judgment. The disciples of Jesus must learn patience and trust God’s timing.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The field is the world: The kingdom of heaven includes all nations (Matthew 28:16–20). 

• The sons of the kingdom are those who obey Jesus (Matthew 13:11–17, Matthew 13:23; Matthew 21:43).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The harvest of judgment, which began with the first coming of the Son of Man (Matthew 3:12) will be completed when he returns (Revelation 14:14–16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: His kingdom: The rule of the Son of Man will be visible over everything at the "end of the age" (Matthew 13:40).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The righteous people will obey God's will as Jesus showed, unlike those "who practice lawlessness" (Matthew 13:41).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Treasure hidden in a field: People buried treasures to protect them from thieves and military enemies (Matthew 25:25). 

• in his joy: Those who find the kingdom of heaven experience more joy from it than any temporary pleasure can offer (see 1 Peter 1:8).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Another mystery of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 13:11) is that it is more valuable than any treasure. So, a person should give up everything to get it (see Matthew 19:21, Matthew 19:29; Philippians 3:7).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This parable is about God's judgment on the last day (Matthew 25:31–46). Then he will forever separate the wicked from the righteous. This warning emphasizes the importance of the two earlier invitations to make a decision to trust Jesus.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The wicked are people who do not obey God's will revealed by Jesus. The righteous are those who obey God's will (see Matthew 5:21–48; Matthew 6:1, Matthew 6:33; Matthew 7:13–27; Matthew 12:33–37; Matthew 16:27).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Understanding the secrets of the kingdom of heaven is a gift from God (Matthew 13:10–17, Matthew 13:23).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• A teacher of religious law who becomes a disciple in the kingdom of God changes allegiance. He now looks to Jesus as the way of salvation.

• new treasures as well as old: This order shows that the new covenant brought by Jesus takes first place. It is greater than the old covenant that God gave through Abraham and Moses (Matthew 5:17–20; Matthew 19:16–22).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: That Jesus was rejected at home is part of the ongoing theme of the Messiah’s rejection by his own people (see chapter Matthew 12; Matthew 15:1–20; Matthew 16:1–12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: carpenter’s son: a carpenter (literally, craftsman) worked with his hands in wood, metal, or stone.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: They felt very insulted. Focusing on the ordinary social status of Jesus (John 6:42), they missed his unique importance.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: To understand the message of Jesus (Matthew 13:10–17) and experience his miracles, you need faith.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Herod Antipas’s official title was tetrarch, which means a ruler of a fourth part of a kingdom. He ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39 (see Matthew 2:19–22). Jesus called Antipas “that fox” (Luke 13:32). John the Baptist rightly condemned him for adultery (Matthew 14:3–12; Luke 3:19–20).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: People were saying that John had been resurrected from the dead (see Matthew 16:14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: John the Baptist’s message drew large crowds, which leaders saw as a political threat (see Josephus, Antiquities 18.5.2). Years after John was executed, many Jews believed that Herod’s military defeat by King Aretas in AD 36 was God’s judgment for killing an innocent man.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: John kept warning Herod about his sin (see Leviticus 18:6; Leviticus 20:21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Herodias's daughter was probably Salome. She would have come from Herodias' earlier marriage to Philip. Such sexually suggestive dances were common among corrupt royalty.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Herod Antipas often made extravagant and foolish promises.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: In ancient times, presenting a head on a tray was a known practice (see Josephus, Antiquities 13.4.8; 14.15.13; 18.5.1; 20.5.1).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: What Jesus did consistently fulfilled Old Testament promises about the kingdom of heaven and the Messiah (Matthew 11:5–6; Matthew 12:28). Here, Jesus reminded people of God's gift of manna to the Israelites (Exodus 16; see John 6:32). This showed that he is the promised prophet of the end times (see Deuteronomy 18:15–16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: About five thousand men were fed, in addition to women and children: At that time, they counted families by the heads of households, not each person.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: After Jesus miraculously fed the crowd, they wanted to make him king (John 6:15). He withdrew from the crowd because it was not the right time.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus showed his power over nature, giving the disciples a chance to trust him as the Son of God (Mathhew 14:33; see also Matthew 8:23–27; Psalm 8:6; Hebrews 2:8–9).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus often went to quiet places to pray, especially during important times in his life and work (Matthew 26:36–46; Mark 1:35; Luke 5:16; Luke 6:12; Luke 9:28).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• During the fourth watch of the night: This was between 3:00 and 6:00 am by Roman timekeeping. 

• Jesus went out … walking on the sea: This act showed God’s rule over the stormy sea (see Job 9:8; Psalm 77:19; Isaiah 43:16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: It is I (literally I am): This statement is associated with the appearance of God himself (see also John 8:24; John 18:5–6; compare Exodus 3:14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: To understand why Jesus performed miracles, refer to the study notes on Matthew 11:5 and 12:28.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The temple was in Jerusalem, which made it the center of authority in Judaism. This gave these ambassadors from the Pharisees and scribes more influence in their discussions with Jesus.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus accused the Pharisees of disobeying God's law because of their focus on preserving traditions.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Jewish teachers developed long-standing traditions to explain how the written Torah should guide daily life. These traditions were memorized and passed from teacher to student by word of mouth(see 1 Corinthians 11:23; 1 Corinthians 15:1–5). 

• break the tradition of … wash their hands (see Mark 7:2–4; Luke 11:38): The tradition of hand washing was seen as important. Ignoring this practice was considered disobedience to the Torah and unfaithfulness to God’s will for Israel (see Matthew 23:25–26).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: A gift devoted to God: The people would probably donate a gift like this at the temple (see Mark 7:11; see also Proverbs 28:24) but it served as a way to avoid financially providing for one's parents.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Nullify: The Pharisees valued their traditions so much that they ignored God's law, turning their devotion into sinful disrespect for God's word.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: You hypocrites! See study note on Matthew 23:13.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• What enters his mouth: Jesus may have been speaking about foods that the law did not allow (such as pork or shellfish) or food made unclean by unwashed hands (Matthew 15:20). 

• What makes a person defiled also makes them unfit to be with God. Jesus moved the focus from outward rules of purity to the true purity of the heart (see Matthew 15:18–19; Matthew 23:25–26; Acts 10:1–48; Romans 14:14).

• A person’s words show their true character (see Matthew 15:18–20; James 3:1–12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: My heavenly Father has not planted: These Pharisees did not belong to the true people of God (see Matthew 3:9–12; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 45:4). God will remove them at the final judgment (see Matthew 3:10; Matthew 8:12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This encounter brings up another debated issue. It is about whether Gentiles (non-Jews) can share in the kingdom of the Messiah (see Matthew 8:11).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Canaanite woman: Matthew uses this old expression to describe the woman as a pagan. 

• Lord, Son of David: The woman seemed to understand that Jesus was the Messiah (see Matthew 1:1; Matthew 9:27; Matthew 17:15; Matthew 20:30).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Did not answer a word: Jesus stayed silent to test the woman's faith (Matthew 5:28; compare Matthew 8:24; Matthew 14:16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jews often referred to pagans as dogs, which were considered ceremonially unclean (Leviticus 11:27). When Jesus spoke to the woman, he was speaking of her condition as a Gentile. She was seen as ceremonially unclean and separated from God (see Matthew 7:6).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Jesus returned to an area with mostly Gentiles (non-Jews) and performed many miracles. Although God mainly sent Jesus for Israel (Matthew 15:21–28), Jesus also started a new era for Gentile salvation (Matthew 1:3, Matthew 1:5–6; Matthew 2:1–12; Matthew 4:12–16; Matthew 8:5–13; Matthew 15:21–28; Matthew 28:16–20). 

• These healings show that God's kingdom began with the work of Jesus (Matthew 8:1–9:34; Matthew 11:5–6; Matthew 12:28).

• the God of Israel: This suggests that the crowd (Matthew 15:30) was mostly Gentile.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The earlier feeding miracle (see Matthew 14:13–21) was for the Jews. This miracle extended the blessing to the gentiles. It continues the theme found in Matthew 15:27. By this miracle, Jesus showed that he is the true "bread of life" (see Matthew 16:5–12; John 6).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Magadan is a place whose location is unknown. It may be the same as Magdala, as some Greek manuscripts say (see also Mark 8:10).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: After being welcomed among the Gentiles (non-Jews), Jesus returned to his own people. There he faced rejection again.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The leaders asked Jesus for a sign from heaven (Matthew 16:1). Jesus made a wordplay with their request. They could read signs in the sky to predict the weather (the Greek word ouranos means both “sky” and “heaven”). But they failed to recognize the Messiah, even though many signs had already been given (see Matthew 11:1–6).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The signs of the times were Jesus himself and the miracles he performed (see Matthew 16:4; Matthew 11:2–6; Matthew 12:28).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus had shown his disciples that he is the true "bread of life" (Matthew 15:32–39; John 6:35, John 6:48). In contrast, the Jewish leaders taught things that were wrong. Their false teaching spread everywhere, like yeast (or leaven) spreads through bread dough (see study note on Matt 16:11–12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Leaven (or yeast) often symbolizes sin and evil (see Exodus 12:8, Exodus 12:15; Leviticus 6:16–17; Galatians 5:9). Here, it represents how deceptive teaching spreads.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Caesarea Philippi was about forty kilometers (twenty-five miles) north of Capernaum. It had many shrines (holy places) dedicated to Pan, the Roman god of nature.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Some, like Herod Antipas, thought Jesus was John the Baptist raised from the dead (Matthew 14:1–2). 

• Others expected Elijah to return before the Messiah came (Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:10–12; Malachi 3:1; Malachi 4:5–6). 

• Jeremiah or one of the prophets: Some thought Jesus was Jeremiah or another prophet. Certain Jews believed Jeremiah would rise again (see 2 Maccabees 15:13–16). Because Jesus spoke strongly on sensitive issues (Matthew 5:17; Matthew 15:1–20), some thought he was Jeremiah. 

At this point, people did not yet understand that Jesus was the Messiah (God’s chosen one).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Peter acknowledges Jesus as "the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Matthew 3:17). This showed that God had opened Peter’s eyes through faith (see Matthew 11:25–27; Matthew 14:33; Matthew 27:54).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: God revealed to Peter his plan for saving people through Jesus, the Messiah. This moment of revelation was key in showing God's will for humanity (see Galatians 1:16; Galatians 3:23; Ephesians 3:5).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• In Greek, Peter’s name is Petros, which means “rock” or “stone.” When Jesus says, on this rock (Greek petra), he is making a play on words between Peter’s name (Petros) and the word for rock (petra).

Peter was the foundational "rock" because he was the first to confess Jesus as the Christ and was leader of the apostles. He was the "founding member" of the Church (see Ephesians 2:20–22; Revelation 21:14). 

Some scholars think Jesus was talking about himself when he mentioned this rock. But it seems Jesus was referring to Peter or Peter's confession. However, it is clearly the church of Jesus, not of Peter. Jesus himself will build it. So, later church leaders do not need to get their authority from Peter. 

• Matthew is the only gospel writer who uses the term "church" (also Matthew 18:17). Here, it means "the community of God’s people" rather than the expanded idea of an organized church. 

• will not prevail against it: The church will not be defeated by Satan's attacks (see Matthew 11:12; Matthew 13:24–30, Matthew 13:36–43).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Keys symbolize access to special knowledge that gives someone authority (see Matthew 13:16–17; Matthew 23:13; Isaiah 22:22; Revelation 3:7). 

• bind … loose: Jesus gave Peter (and later the rest of the twelve apostles, Matthew 18:18) the authority to teach God's will as Jesus Christ revealed it (Matthew 13:52; Matthew 18:15–20; Matthew 23:2–12; Matthew 28:16–20). 

• will be: You could also translate this as will have been. This emphasizes that God’s sovereign decision comes first.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• This is the first of three times Jesus told his disciples that he would suffer. He said he would be betrayed, crucified, and killed (see also Matthew 17:22–23; Matthew 20:18–19). Each of these predictions also taught a lesson about the cost of following him (see Matthew 16:24–27; Matthew 20:20–28). 

• The suffering of Jesus was part of God’s plan and was necessary for the Messiah (see Matthew 17:12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus was now officially recognized by his disciples as the Messiah. He then began to reveal a surprising part of his mission. He must suffer before entering his glory (Matthew 16:21–23). Those who follow him will also face suffering (Matthew 16:24–28).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: began to rebuke Him: Peter realized that Jesus was God's Messiah. But he did not understand that the Messiah had to suffer.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Just as Satan tempted Jesus to take royal privileges without first going to the cross (see Matthew 4:8–10), so now Jesus saw Peter’s words as stirred up by satanic forces.

• a stumbling block: This is something that causes a person to fall.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• deny … take up … follow: These three commands symbolize an extreme commitment. They mean confessing sins to God with humility, giving personal goals to God, and living by his will (see also Matthew 5:20; Matthew 10:34–39; Matthew 18:1–5; Matthew 20:20–28). 

• take up his cross: This is a metaphor for devotion (see Luke 9:23). It is not necessarily a command to die for one's faith, though that is always a possibility for the disciples of Jesus (Matthew 5:10–12; Matthew 10:21). 

• Matthew uses follow both literally (see Matthew 9:19; Matthew 26:58) and as a metaphor. Metaphorically, it shows interest in a teacher (Matthew 4:25; Matthew 8:1, Matthew 8:10; Matthew 12:15; Matthew 14:13; Matthew 19:2; Matthew 20:29; Matthew 21:9) or personal loyalty to Jesus. This involves him summoning, a response to commit, and significant ongoing struggles (Matthew 4:20, Matthew 4:22; Matthew 8:19, Matthew 8:22–23; Matthew 9:9; Matthew 10:38; Matthew 16:24; Matthew 19:21, Matthew 19:27).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The disciples of Jesus need to give up control of their own lives, even being willing to suffer or die for him. Jesus promised that those who follow him in this way may suffer now, but at the final judgment God will show them to be right, clear away every false charge, and welcome them into his kingdom with honor (see 1 Peter 2:23).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: His soul: "Soul" and "life" (Matthew 16:25) both translate the same Greek word psuchē. It refers to the essence or being of a person—the self.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The command to deny oneself and follow Jesus has its basis in the fact that Jesus will return to judge all people according to what they have done (see Matthew 19:28; Matthew 24:29–31; Matthew 25:31; Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12).

entries.title: Matthew
Matthew
entries.content:
• Peter, James, and John later went with Jesus to Gethsemane (Matthew 26:37; 2 Peter 1:16–19). 

• We cannot know the exact location of this high mountain. The traditional site, Mount Tabor, is about 580 meters high (1,900 feet). It is not on the way if leaving from Caesarea Philippi (Matthew 16:13) to go to Capernaum (Matthew 17:24). 

Mount Hermon is another option. It is about 2,800 meters high (9,200 feet) and located in Syria, about sixty-four kilometers (forty miles) north of Capernaum. Yet, it is improbable that “scribes” (Mark 9:14) would have gathered at the base of a mountain in non-Jewish territory. A likely location is Mount Meron, about 1,220 meters high (4,000 feet). It is located between Caesarea Philippi and Capernaum.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: He was transfigured: In this moment, the inner and divine nature of Jesus, normally hidden, was now revealed. The three disciples were given a glimpse of his glory (see Exodus 34:29–35; Psalm 104:2; 2 Corinthians 3:12–18; Revelation 1:16). All of the disciples of Jesus will share in this glory one day (Matthew 13:43).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Moses represents the law, and Elijah represents the prophets. They appeared as witnesses to Christ. Their presence showed that Jesus, the Son of God, fulfills everything written in the law and the prophets (see Matthew 5:17–20; Matthew 11:2–6; Matthew 12:28).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Three shelters (Or three tabernacles): Peter probably thought the kingdom of heaven was about to arrive in full glory (compare Acts 1:6). He wanted to remember the moment by building shelters.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• A bright cloud enveloped them: In the Old Testament, a cloud often showed God’s presence with Israel during the time of Moses (see Exodus 24:15–18; Exodus 25:8; Exodus 29:45–46; Exodus 40:34–38). 

• My beloved Son: This confirmed what Peter had already declared about Jesus (Matthew 16:16–17). 

• The disciples were told to listen to Jesus because he is God’s Son. As a prophet, he reveals God’s will (Matthew 11:27; see Deuteronomy 18:15, Deuteronomy 18:18; Acts 3:22–23; Acts 7:37).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: People often react this way when they experience God's glory (for example, Isaiah 6:5; Daniel 8:17; Daniel 10:9, Daniel 10:15–19; Revelation 1:17).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: People could not fully understand Jesus until he completed his work, especially his death and resurrection.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Elijah’s appearance made the disciples ask about the belief that Elijah must return before the Messiah comes (see Malachi 4:5–6). Jesus pointed to John the Baptist as the one who fulfilled that role. In doing so, he reminded them of the surprising truth that the Messiah must suffer, just as John, his forerunner, had also suffered (Matthew 14:3–12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: O unbelieving and perverse generation: This phrase often describes moral corruption (see Deuteronomy 32:5, Deuteronomy 32:19–22). Jesus usually directed this exclamation at unbelieving Jewish crowds or leaders who refused to recognize God's presence in him (see Matthew 12:39). But here the phrase sharply criticizes his disciples for not trusting in Jesus and his power to save and heal.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Here, the phrase so little faith means the same as no faith. 

• faith the size of a mustard seed: This suggests that even a tiny amount of faith can help the disciples achieve great things (Hebrews 21:21; compare 1 Corinthians 13:2). It also suggests that if they let their faith increase (see Matthew 13:31–32), they could act with strong belief.

• "Moving mountains" is a saying that means overcoming obstacles and achieving God's goals (Isaiah 40:4; Isaiah 49:11; Isaiah 54:10; 1 Corinthians 13:2).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: be delivered: See Matthew 20:18; Matthew 26:14–16, Matthew 26:45–49 to see how this prophecy came true.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Every adult citizen of Israel had to pay the temple tax of one-half shekel. This was a coin weighing 4 grams. In the time of Jesus, priests and some rabbis did not pay this tax. 

• Peter spoke on behalf of the twelve apostles (see Matthew 10:2).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: As an obedient Jew, Jesus would have paid the tax every year, and he did pay it. The lesson Jesus wanted to teach was that as God's Son, he is greater than the temple (Matthew 12:5–6). By this, he showed that a decisive break with the temple was coming (see Matthew 16:18–19; Matthew 21:33–46).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
At that time: Matthew connects the disciples' questions to the earlier teaching about the temple. The disciples started to think their new freedom from Jewish authority gave them their own authority. 

Jesus had also spoken about special revelations (Matthew 11:25–27; Matthew 13:11–17) and about leadership roles (Matthew 10:2–4; Matthew 19:28). This may have caused jealousy and arguments about power among the disciples. Their disputes may have centered on the importance of Peter (Matthew 17:25) or the special place of Peter, James, and John (Matthew 17:1–3).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
This fourth major teaching in Matthew (see study note on Matthew 5:1–7:29) focuses on how people responded to the Messiah. The disciples accepted him, while the Jewish leaders and most people did not. As this division increased, Jesus taught his disciples about community life. 

To follow the standards of Jesus, a community should live with:

• humility (Matthew 18:1–5), 

• sensitivity (Matthew 18:6–9), 

• compassion (Matthew 18:10–14), 

• discipline (Matthew 18:15–18), and 

• forgiveness (Matthew 18:21–35). 

Like the other teachings, a closing statement (Matthew 19:1–2) connects to the next section.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Like little children means being humble (Matthew 18:4). The disciples had been focused on status and ambition.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus then talked about unity in the community. Welcoming a humble disciple of Jesus is the same as welcoming Jesus himself (see Matthew 10:40–42).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Cause one … to stumble: This means to lead believers to turn away from Christ, whether children or adults who have become “like children” in faith (see Matthew 18:3). 

• The title little ones emphasizes their humility (see Matthew 5:3–12; Matthew 18:4; Matthew 19:13–15). 

• The thought of being drowned with a large millstone around the neck is terrifying. But Jesus warned that causing someone to lose faith will bring even greater suffering (Matthew 18:7; Matthew 26:24; Revelation 18:21; Matthew 22:13).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus shifts his concern to the person. You must remove anything that leads you to sin (see Matthew 5:29–30; Colossians 3:5–17).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Do not look down on any of these: This can happen by refusing to welcome them (Matthew 18:5–6) or by not providing pastoral care when needed (Matthew 18:12–14; see Matthew 19:13–15). 

• their angels: See Matthew 4:5–7; Hebrews 1:14.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Just as a shepherd works to find a lost sheep, we must not despise or ignore the “little ones” (Matthew 18:6).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The shepherd's joy is the same as the Father's joy. The goal of pastoral care is to ensure God keeps all his sheep.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: If another believer sins, love means we should talk to them privately and point out the wrong (Leviticus 19:17; Luke 17:3; Galatians 6:1; 1 Timothy 5:20; Titus 3:10).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Resolving issues should be private at first and only made public if absolutely necessary.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The community of believers should stay united and avoid conflicts. Members should seek reconciliation (Matthew 18:15–20) and be ready to forgive (Matthew 18:21–35). Sometimes, strict discipline might be necessary (Matthew 18:17).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: By requiring one or two others to be present, Jesus stopped slander and false accusations among the congregation (see John 8:17; 2 Corinthians 13:1; 1 Timothy 5:19; Hebrews 10:28).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The church is the local Christian community. 

• An unrepentant person (someone refusing to turn from sin) is to be treated as an outsider, like a lawbreaker. Excluding a person from fellowship (sometimes called excommunication) comes from the belief that God’s people must be holy (Acts 5:1–6; Romans 16:17; 1 Corinthians 5:1–13; 2 Corinthians 6:14–18; Galatians 5:7–12; 2 Thessalonians 3:14–15). Sin harms fellowship with both other believers and with God. The goal is not revenge or control, but to restore the sinner to holiness and community (Matthew 18:10–15; Galatians 6:1; James 5:19–20).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Bind … loose: The privilege and authority Jesus gave to Peter (Matthew 16:19) are here given to the church (or possibly to the twelve apostles, Matthew 18:1). The community's decisions, when they are in agreement with God's will, are eternally binding.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: These sayings guide how to discipline and restore members in the community of disciples.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Anything you ask for: In the context of church discipline (Matthew 18:15–17), this means discipline must be done in a prayerful way.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Christ is present in the process of church discipline, so this process confirms God's decision.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Peter thought forgiving seven times was generous, but Jesus surprised him. A disciple should graciously forgive like God does, without limits and freely (see Matthew 18:10–14). If someone does not forgive in this way, it shows they have not experienced God's forgiveness for themselves (Matthew 18:35; see Matthew 6:12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Seventy-seven times: sus teaches that forgiveness should have no limit. His followers must forgive sincerely, not only in words but also in attitude and actions (Matthew 18:35; see also Genesis 4:23–24).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Ten thousand talents: The talent was the largest unit of currency, but its value changed over time. This debt was impossible to repay. This amount was more than all of Galilee's tax revenue.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: I will pay back everything: the slave's promise to pay the huge debt emphasizes the king's great mercy and the slave's lack of forgiveness (Matthew 18:29–30).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: A hundred denarii: The first servant owed a debt about one million times larger than this amount owed to him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• This is how God reacts to those who refuse to forgive (Matthew 18:35). 

• until he should repay all that he owed: This means permanently, because he could never repay the debt.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: That is how My heavenly Father will treat each of you: Prison and torture (Matthew 18:34) is a metaphor for hell (see Matthew 5:22).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus was traveling to Jerusalem (Matthew 19:1; Matthew 20:29; Matthew 21:1). This was another chance to teach the disciples what it means to be his disciples.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
There were two different opinions on when a man could divorce his wife: 

• One group of Pharisees, following Rabbi Shammai, believed divorce was only allowable for adultery or serious wrongdoing. 

• The other group, following Rabbi Hillel, thought a man could divorce his wife for any reason, even if she burned his dinner.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Pharisees did not consider all of God's teachings. God intended marriage to be a permanent union (see Genesis 2:18–25; see also 1 Corinthians 7:10–16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Since God created marriage as a union, people do not have the right to end it. Jesus confirmed that divorce should not happen.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Why … did Moses order: The Pharisees believed Jesus contradicted a command in the law (see Deuteronomy 24:1–4). But Moses allowed divorce only because of people's stubbornness. Jesus introduced the radical idea that what God permits is not always what he desires (see 1 Corinthians 6:12). Divorce is never what God desires (Malachi 2:14–16). It shows the brokenness of human sin.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Jesus allows only one valid reason for a man to divorce: if his wife has been unfaithful (see Matthew 5:32). For those who thought divorce was easy, Jesus emphasizes God's created order. Marriage is meant to last forever (see Mark 10:11–12). 

• commits adultery: This refers to a man who divorces his wife without a valid reason. If he remarries, it is the same as adultery. Jesus aims to reestablish that marriage is permanent.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This statement refers to what the disciples said in Matthew 19:10.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Eunuchs are men who cannot physically have children, either because of a birth defect or because they were made unable through surgery (castration). Jesus also used the word in a figurative way for those who choose not to marry (see Luke 14:26; Luke 18:29; 1 Corinthians 7:7–8). 

• for the sake of the kingdom of Heaven: Jesus was not criticizing marriage. He meant that unmarried people often have more freedom for ministry (see 1 Corinthians 7:25–35).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Jesus would place his hands on others to bless them (see Luke 4:40; Luke 13:13; see also Genesis 48:14–15; Acts 19:6). 

• The disciples tried to stop the parents from bringing children to Jesus. They wanted to protect him, but their action showed the wrong attitude toward children (see Matthew 18:5–6, Matthew 18:10).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Why do you ask Me: as a Jew, the man should have known that God shows his standard of goodness in his commandments. The man's questions show he did not trust God's revealed will (also Matthew 19:20). 

• there is only One who is good: The man might have thought he could be perfectly good on his own, but only God is the truly good. So, God is from where all goodness comes.

• keep the commandments: Jesus might be trying to show the man his own sinfulness by asking him to do the impossible. Or more probably, he is restating that good works are the clear measure of how true a person's faith is (see Matthew 7:13–27).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: When Jesus told the man to go, sell … come, follow, Jesus revealed that the man had not truly followed the first of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:3). His possessions (his wealth and security) had become his god (see Matthew 6:20, Matthew 6:24; Matthew 13:44–46).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Jesus teaches a lesson about discipleship from the rich man's sad refusal. It is difficult for the rich to humble themselves, admit their needs, and trust in God (see Matthew 5:3; Luke 6:24; 1 Timothy 6:9–10). 

• The kingdom of heaven here means eternal life (Matthew 19:16–17, Matthew 19:29) or salvation as a result of God's renewing work (Matthew 19:25–26).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Easier for a camel: This analogy emphasizes how difficult it is for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. Some manuscripts use a Greek word meaning rope (kamilos) instead of camel (kamēlos), a difference of only one letter. 

• to pass through the eye of a needle: This image suggests it is impossible for wealthy people to enter the kingdom of God. But the situation is not completely hopeless (Matthew 19:26–27). See study note on Mark 10:25.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: God's renewing grace is completely essential for the wealthy to be able to repent from making wealth an idol, give up their possessions if needed, and follow Jesus (Matthew 19:21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• You … will also sit on twelve thrones: The disciples will share in judging. This is a reversal, where those who are rich and powerful now will be judged by those who are humble and poor (see Matthew 19:30). 

• Judging can mean both ruling with authority and condemning for wrongdoing (see Revelation 20:4).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This parable is like the parable of the lost son (Luke 15:11–32). In both, God shows grace to two groups, but one complains about unfair treatment.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Workers received their pay at the end of the day (Deuteronomy 24:14–15).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: See Matthew 5:19 and Matthew 8:11–12.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This mother's question seems to have come from her sons, as Jesus answered the sons instead of the mother (compare Mark 10:35–37).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Each time Jesus predicted his suffering in the Gospel of Matthew, he also gave teaching about what it means to be his disciple. These teachings showed that discipleship is shaped by Jesus own path of service and sacrifice (see Matthew 16:24–28; Matthew 17:24–18:5). This teaching called the Messiah's disciples to imitate his service and sacrifice.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus had already promised positions of authority in God’s kingdom to the disciples (Matthew 19:28). The request of the two brothers came from selfish desire to be important, without concern for the suffering the Messiah would soon face (see Matthew 23:6; Luke 14:7–11).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The cup refers to the duty duty, calling, and destiny of Jesus (see Matthew 26:39; John 18:11; also Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17, Isaiah 51:22; Revelation 16:19).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: You will indeed: James eventually died for his faith (Acts 12:2). John suffered severe persecution (Acts 4:3; Acts 5:40; Revelation 1:9).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The ten … they were indignant: This shows that selfish ambition was not only in James and John. The other disciples also struggled with it (see also Matthew 21:15; Matthew 26:8; Luke 13:14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Rulers who do not know God often desire power and control. But those who follow the Son of Man should not act this way (Matthew 18:1–5; Matthew 19:13–15; Matthew 23:1–12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Often the word slave is a metaphor that describes a disciple's submissive relationship to their master (Matthew 8:9; Matthew 10:24–25; Matthew 24:45–51; Matthew 25:14–30). The disciples of Jesus serve others, following his example (for example, John 13:1–17).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The phrase the Son of Man … come: This expression suggests that Jesus already existed before his birth on earth. It points back to Daniel’s vision of the Son of Man coming from heaven to receive authority and glory (see Daniel 7:13–14). 

• as a ransom for many: Jesus said he would freely give his life as a payment to rescue many people. His death brought freedom from the power and penalty of sin (see Matthew 26:26–29; Isaiah 53:10–12; Romans 3:24). In this way, he bought them out of slavery to sin (see Galatians 5:1).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The blind men’s expression of faith in the Son of David was an acknowledgment of Jesus as the Messiah (see Matthew 21:9; Matthew 22:42; 2 Samuel 7:12–16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Bethphage is a Hebrew name that means house of figs. It was probably on the east side of the Mount of Olives, between Bethany and Jerusalem.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus entering Jerusalem starts Matthew's story of how the Messiah's suffering and resurrection establish salvation.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus was revealing himself as the Lord who, as king of Israel, goes up to Mount Zion on a donkey (Matthew 21:5; see Zechariah 9:9).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This part of the Old Testament fulfillment emphasizes the Messiah's peaceful, humble, and saving work (see Matthew 11:28–30; Isaiah 62:11; Zechariah 9:9–10).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The crowds with Jesus saw him as a prophet, empowered by God to teach and perform miracles. 

• The mention from Nazareth in Galilee emphasizes the humble beginnings of Jesus (see Matthew 2:23).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Buying and selling happened in the temple complex, in the Court of the Gentiles. 

• Money changers made profit by exchanging foreign money into the official Jewish currency. Jesus criticized this commercial activity because it dishonored the holiness of the temple (see Mark 11:11–18).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The close association of the temple cleansing (see John 2:13–16) and the cursing of the fig tree (Matthew 21:18–19) shows Jesus as the Messiah (God’s chosen one). He confronted Israel and warned that God judges those who reject the Messiah and his message.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: What Jesus did was right because people were using money in a way that desecrated God's glory.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Jewish leaders’ refusal to believe is contrasted with the joyful faith and praise of little children (see Matthew 18:1–14; Matthew 19:13–15).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Have you never read: Jesus asked this challenging question to opponents who failed to see that his ministry fulfilled the promises about the Messiah (see also Matthew 12:3, Matthew 12:5; Matthew 19:4; Matthew 21:42; Matthew 22:31).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Nothing on it except leaves: Mark notes that "it was not the season for figs" (see Mark 11:13). It was spring, just before Passover. Figs start growing in spring but ripen in fall. 

• immediately the tree withered: Matthew seems to have shortened the story (compare Matthew 21:18–22; Mark 11:13–14, Mark 11:20–23). The cursing of the fig tree symbolizes God's judgment on Israel for rejecting the Messiah (see Matt 3:9; Matthew 8:11–12). The Israelites are like a fig tree that looks promising but has no fruit. This was especially true of the hypocritical leaders. They did not bear fruit, symbolic of receiving the Messiah (see Matthew 21:33–46).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus was encouraging the disciples to trust in God and pray with faith. He was not promising that God would approve everything they might desire (1 John 5:14–15).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Elders of the people: This refers to the family leaders from each tribe. They were part of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council in Jerusalem (compare Ezra 5:5; Ezra 6:14; Ezra 10:8).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This section focuses on how Jewish leaders challenged the authority of Jesus. Each time, the wisdom of Jesus revealed their lack of spiritual understanding. These debates also revealed the status of Jesus as the Messiah and the consequences of rejecting him. Sadly, the leaders became more resistant with each encounter and plotted to kill Jesus (Matthew 21:23, Matthew 21:46; Matthew 22:15–17, Matthew 22:23, Matthew 22:34, Matthew 22:41).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus gave a riddle. The answer solved the leaders’ question and placed them in a dilemma that showed what was in their hearts (Matthew 21:25–26). Asking a counter-question was common in debates at that time.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The minsitry of John, like the ministry of Jesus, was controversial (see Matthew 3:1, Matthew 3:5–6). This was true especially after John publicly criticized Herod Antipas for his sins (see Matthew 14:4). The Jewish leaders did not want to admit that John's work was from God. They had refused to believe John and repent of their sins (Matthew 3:2). They also refused to accept Jesus as the Messiah (John 1:29–34).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Jewish leaders did not have the honesty or bravery to admit their beliefs about John. So, it was fair for Jesus not to answer their question.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This parable continues to emphasize why John is important.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Three parables expose the guilt of those who rejected the Messiah and lost their special status as God's chosen people. God now considers only those who accept Jesus as the Messiah as his people.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: I will not: This response must have offended Jews who learned from a young age to show respect for the authority of a father (see Matthew 8:21–22).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The right way to live is to follow the will of God (Matthew 3:15; Matthew 5:20; see also Proverbs 8:20; Proverbs 12:28).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: In this story, Jesus refers back to Isaiah 5:1–7. The people of Israel who rejected God's Messiah lost the privilege of being God's people. Now, God has called the Christian community, made up of both Jews and Gentiles (non-Jews), to be his people (see Romans 9:4–8; Romans 11:1–12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: He sent his servants: The prophets had spoken God's message to Israel. In this parable, the tenant farmers represent Israel's leaders, whom Jesus blamed for killing God's prophets (Matthew 23:29–37).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Finally: God's revelation reached its goal in Jesus (see Matthew 13:16–17; Hebrews 1:1–2).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: when the owner of the vineyard returns: The vineyard owner's return symbolizes the Lord's coming for judgment (see Matthew 16:27; Matthew 24:1–36).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Jewish religious leaders declared their own condemnation.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The cornerstone was either the first stone of the foundation or the last stone placed, like the top of an arch. The builders rejected this stone as unworthy, but it was actually the most important. Jesus was talking about his role in the kingdom of God (Matthew 21:43) and how the Jewish religious leaders rejected him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Taken away from you: Either the privilege of being God’s chosen nation no longer belonged to the Jews, or the religious leaders had lost the privilege of being leaders of God’s people (see Romans 9–11). 

• The Christian community is a nation that will produce the proper "fruit" or right results. This means a life of trust and obedience that shows the start of God's kingdom (see Matthew 3:8; Matthew 7:15–20; Matthew 12:33; Matthew 13:8, Matthew 13:26).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Those who opposed the Messiah would soon win a temporary victory. But the Messiah would eventually defeat them. The stone would crush them because the death of Jesus on the cross led to his vindication and triumph (see also Daniel 2:34–35, Daniel 2:44–45).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This explanation fits with Matthew’s theme of God’s judgment on the Jewish leaders who misled the people of Israel (see Matthew 23:13–15).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: In this parable, Israel had often rejected God’s message in the past. In the same way, Israel rejected the Messiah and faced judgment. In Israel’s place, God raised up the church (Matthew 16:17–19; Matthew 21:43). God also expects the church to live in righteousness (Romans 11:11–24).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The king represents God, and his son is Jesus (Galatians 4:4; Hebrews 1:1–2). 

• The feast represents the kingdom of the Messiah.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: those he had invited: This refers to the nation of Israel. They ignored God's servants, the prophets (see study note on Matthew 21:33–46).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus was referring to the future destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (see Matthew 23:37–39; Matthew 24:2).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: People who refuse God's invitation do not deserve to enter his kingdom (see Matthew 3:8; Matthew 10:13, Matthew 10:37–38).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: as many as you can find: God's invitation is now open to all people, not only the nation of Israel (see Matthew 28:16–20; compare Matthew 10:5–6; Matthew 15:21–28).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: both evil and good: See Matthew 13:24–50.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Wearing the right clothes symbolizes spiritual qualities that show true faith (see Matthew 7:13–27).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• weeping and gnashing of teeth: This phrase describes the intense pain and sorrow that come from being condemned for sin and unbelief (see Matthew 8:12; Matthew 13:42, Matthew 13:50; Matthew 24:51; Matthew 25:30). 

• outer darkness: This is a picture of eternal punishment, shown as being far from God’s presence.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Many people receive an invitation to the kingdom. But God only choses a few who faithfully obey Jesus.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: In first-century Palestine, debates about Roman taxes were intense (see also Matthew 17:24–27).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Pharisees were strict Jewish leaders who opposed Roman rule. They strongly resisted Roman control and wanted to protect Jewish traditions and independence. They usually disagreed with the supporters of Herod. But in this case, they joined together because both groups hated Jesus.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Is it lawful … or not?: They asked the question to try and trap Jesus. If he said no, they could arrest him for rebelling against Rome. If he said yes, they could accuse him of supporting Roman oppression.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: You hypocrites: See study note on Matthew 23:13.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The people had to pay the poll tax with the denarius coin. This coin showed the picture and title of Caesar (the Roman emperor). Old Testament rules against worshiping images (Exodus 20:4; Leviticus 26:1; Deuteronomy 4:15–24) made this coin controversial for Jews (see Josephus, War 2.9.2–3). To avoid conflict, some Roman governors in Palestine minted coins without human images. This showed respect for Jewish religious concerns.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus answered with wisdom. He said people should give Caesar the honor that belongs to him, but they must give God the greater honor and loyalty. Being loyal to God does not always mean being disloyal to human rulers. Jesus showed that there are two realms of authority, Caesar’s and God’s, and God’s authority is greater (Acts 4:19).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Sadducees (see Matthew 3:7) described a situation about levirate marriage. This was a Jewish custom where a man marries his brother's widow (see Genesis 38:6–11; Deuteronomy 25:5–6). They tried to use this as proof that resurrection from the dead is impossible.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The resurrection was an important topic in the time of Jesus. But the people only asked about it to try and trap him.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: the power of God: This probably means God's ability to resurrect people who have died.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: like the angels in heaven: Jesus was not teaching that people will be without gender in heaven. Nor was he criticizing God's order of marriage and sexuality. Instead, he was confirming that God will transform people into a glorious new existence (see 1 Corinthians 15:35–49; 2 Corinthians 5:1–5). In this new existence, parts of the current world, like marriage, will not be present.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: God spoke of himself as the God of Abraham in the present tense. This shows that Abraham is still alive and that there will be a resurrection.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Many strict Jews believed that every commandment was equally important. Because of this, a careless answer to the question could lead to an accusation of rejecting God’s law.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus answers using the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–9), a key statement of God's covenant with Israel. The first Hebrew word in Deuteronomy 6:4–9 is shema‘, meaning "hear!"

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Love your neighbor as yourself: Leviticus 19:18; see also Romans 13:9; Galatians 5:6, Galatians 5:14; James 2:8.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: hang on: The words of Jesus showed that God’s will is unified and consistent, as it is recorded in Scripture.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: After Jesus defended himself against the traps of his opponents (Matthew 21:23–22:40), he asked them a question. How can the Messiah be called both the son of David and also the Lord of David (Psalm 110:1).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Whose son is He? … David's: See study note on Matthew 9:27; also see 2 Samuel 7:12–14; Psalms 2:7–9; Psalms 110:110; Isaiah 11:1, Isaiah 11:10; Jeremiah 23:5–6.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The quote is from Psalm 110:1 and New Testament writers often use it to describe Jesus (see Acts 2:34–35; 1 Corinthians 15:25; Hebrews 1:13; Hebrews 2:8; Hebrews 10:12–13; Revelation 3:21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: how can He be David’s son?: The answer is that Jesus is not only the son of David; he is also the Son of God (Matthew 14:33).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: No one could answer him because they had never thought the Messiah would be God as a human being in the flesh (see John 1:1–14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Jewish religious leaders tried to find a reason to accuse Jesus publicly but could not (Matthew 21:23–22:46). Jesus then addressed the crowds and his disciples to openly criticize the religious leaders for often failing to obey God's righteous standards.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This last extended teaching (see study note on Matthew 5:1–7:29) focuses on the judgment awaiting those who reject the Messiah.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat: This means that they give authoritative explanations about the law of Moses. They passed down oral traditions associated with the law and thought to be from Moses. They judged religious and social issues based on these traditions (see Matthew 15:2).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: practice and obey: This was not a full confirmation of everything the Pharisees taught (see Matthew 15:1–20; Matthew 16:5–12; Matthew 23:13–39). It might refer only to teachings that agreed with the law of Moses, or it could be bitter irony or sarcasm. Jesus might also have advised conforming to the Pharisees’ teachings to avoid causing offense (Matthew 17:24–27).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• heavy, burdensome loads: According to the rabbis, there were 613 laws with commands and prohibitions (see Matthew 11:28–30; Acts 15:10, Acts 15:28). 

• not willing to lift a finger: The religious leaders were not willing to ease or change these traditional laws.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• phylacteries: Pious Jews sometimes wore small prayer boxes, called phylacteries. These were placed on the head and the upper left arm. Inside were written copies of important Old Testament commands (see Deuteronomy 6:6–9; Deuteronomy 11:18–19). 

• Another custom was wearing tassels, which were also a sign of devotion (see Matthew 9:20; see also Numbers 15:38–41). Some made their tassels extra long to draw attention to their religious devotion.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: the chief seats in the synagogue: These were close to the Torah scrolls and faced the congregation.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Rabbi was a title given to an authoritative and respected Jewish teacher.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Rabbi: In Judaism, these men were authoritative mediators for sharing knowledge about God (see Matthew 23:7). But under the new covenant, there is only one authoritative teacher, Jesus himself as the Messiah (see Jeremiah 31:31–34).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus does not forbid using titles (especially for one's father). Instead, he warns against claiming undue honor when teaching about God. In the community of Jesus, everyone is equal and knows God (see Matthew 12:46–50; Matthew 18:15–20). The titles Rabbi, Father, and Teacher are similar in meaning.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Later Jewish writings show that people respected teachers by calling them Father (see, for example, Mishnah Eduyyoth Matthew 1:4). 

• one Father: See Matthew 6:9; Malachi 2:10; compare 1 Corinthians 4:15.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Instructor: This title means the role and office of guiding others to understand God. Jesus, not the scribes and Pharisees, is the teacher of God's will (Matthew 5:17).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The disciples of Jesus should lead by serving others, in distinct contrast to Israel's religious leaders (described in Matthew 23:5–7).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Woe to you: This is a distinct warning about God's judgment. 

• hypocrites!: In English, hypocrisy means a contradiction between what is real and what seems to be real. In the Bible, it means misunderstanding God's will, misleading others, and facing God's judgment. This often includes: desire for fame and power (Matthew 23:5–12), misuse of teaching authority, false teachings (Matthew 23:13–22), and focusing on minor ethical details (Matthew 23:23–28).

A suitable English word for these behaviors is heresy. The Pharisees and religious teachers showed these traits. As the Christian church grew, these traits continued to appear (for example, 1 Timothy 4:1–3; 2 Peter 2:1–22). So God's children must always be on guard against them (James 4:7–10; 1 Peter 2:1–3). 

• you shut the kingdom: This comes through their false teachings and opposition to Jesus (see Matthew 9:32–34; Matthew 12:22–37; Matthew 15:12–14; Matthew 21:15; John 9:13–34). The Jewish religious teachers and Pharisees stopped others from hearing and believing the truth about the Messiah.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Matthew gathered seven warnings of sorrow to come (literally woe to you) inspired by similar Old Testament lists (Isaiah 5:8–23; Habakkuk 2:6–20). Matthew arranged them to reach a climax with the killing of the prophets.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• A convert (proselyte) fully accepted Judaism by performing ceremonies like baptism, sacrifice, and circumcision (see Acts 13:43). 

A convert differed from a "God-fearer." A God-fearer was a person who accepted some Jewish beliefs, especially monotheism (belief in one God), without fully converting to Judaism (see Luke 7:4–5; Acts 10:2). To win a single convert likely means persuading God-fearers to fully convert by becoming circumcised (compare Galatians 2:3, Galatians 2:14; Matthew 5:2–12; Matthew 6:12–13). 

• of hell: The Greek word here is Gehenna. It was a valley outside Jerusalem used as a place of burning; See study note on Matthew 5:29.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The religious leaders said that some oaths were less binding, and this allowed them to deceive people. But Jesus called for honesty and for keeping every commitment (see Matthew 5:33–37).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Jewish teachers of religious law and Pharisees believed that careful and precise tithing showed their dedication to the law. Without denying the importance of tithing, Jesus revealed that they completely ignored the more important parts of the law (Isaiah 1:16–17; Jeremiah 22:3; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:8; Zechariah 7:9).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: gnat … camel: In Aramaic, the language Jesus likely spoke, these two words sound similar (qalma … gamla). This makes a wordplay or pun. Jesus used the contrast between a tiny gnat and a huge camel to show the hypocrisy of focusing on small details while ignoring much greater issues.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: If a person is pure inside, it leads to doing the right things. But doing the right things does not make a person pure inside (Matthew 6:19–34; Matthew 12:33–37; Matthew 15:15–20).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jewish people used to coat limestone tombs, like funerary urns or ossuaries, with a mixture of marble and lime. This filled the holes and made the tombs look nicer. It also helped visitors to Jerusalem see and avoid them, preventing contamination. Jesus did not criticize decorating tombs. Instead, he compared these whitewashed tombs to Jewish religious teachers and Pharisees. Both looked good on the outside but had contamination and impurity on the inside.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: By building and decorating the tombs for the prophets, the teachers of religious law and Pharisees showed outward support for the prophets. But inwardly they were of the same sinful character as their ancestors who had murdered the prophets.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Fill up, then, the measure of the sin of your fathers: By killing God's Messiah, they would complete Israel's history of killing God's prophets (see 1 Thessalonians 2:14–16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This covers the first and last murders recorded in the Hebrew Bible. Abel was killed in Genesis 4:8–11, and Zechariah in 2 Chronicles 24:15–22, which is the last book in the Hebrew Bible order. Jesus implies that his generation would be held guilty for all the murders of God’s righteous servants in the Old Testament (compare Matt 27:25).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Even though Jesus had just given a severe judgment against Israel (Matthew 23:29–36), he truly wanted them to repent and accept God's grace. 

• as a hen: This is an image of protective care (see also Deuteronomy 32:11; Ruth 2:12; Psalms 17:8; Psalms 36:7; Psalms 57:1; Psalms 61:4; Psalms 91:4).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: your house is left to you desolate: God would leave the temple (Ezekiel 10:18–19; Ezekiel 11:22–23; compare Matthew 1:23). Then God would allow the destruction of both the temple and Jerusalem.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord: his may point to a future time when the nation of Israel will turn to the Messiah (see also Romans 11:12–32).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The architecture of the temple was a source of pride for the Jewish people (see study note on Mark 13:1).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Some think chapter Matthew 24:24 is about the return of Jesus at the end of time. Others think it as a prediction of events in AD 70, when the Romans destroyed Jerusalem and the temple. Some think it refers to both events. See also study notes on Mark 13.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: not one stone: The destruction of Jerusalem and the temple showed God's judgment against Israel (see 1 Kings 9:7–9; Jeremiah 7:8–15; Jeremiah 9:10–12; Jeremiah 26:6, Jeremiah 26:18; Micah 3:12; see also Isaiah 64:11; Luke 19:44; Acts 6:14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The Greek word parousia means coming or appearing. 

• end of the age (or end of the world): This phrase refers to the final end of a period in salvation history (see Matthew 13:39–40, Matthew 13:49; also Hebrews 9:26). The second coming of Jesus will end normal history with a final judgment. The disciples believed the temple's destruction and the end of history had a close link.

entries.title: Matthew
