entries.content: Jesus warned his disciples not to be tricked by false messiahs and not to lose hope when disasters come. These things do not mean the end has come right away. History must follow the course God has set. The signs in Matthew 24:4–8 are not the end themselves but events that come before the end.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: claiming, ‘I am the Christ,’: During AD 30 to 70, many false prophets and miracle workers claimed to be the Messiah. They convinced people to follow them, promising salvation (Josephus, Antiquities 18.4.1; 20.5.1; 20.8.6; War 6.5.2). The first known person to openly claim to be the Messiah was Bar Kochba in AD 132. It is unclear if Jesus was talking about impostors before the temple's destruction, false messiahs throughout the church Age, or possibly during a future difficult time.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• These things must happen: This shows that times of trouble are part of God’s plan as he moves history toward its conclusion (see Matthew 24:7, Matthew 24:29–30; 2 Thessalonians 2:8–12). 

• the end: This might mean the end of a period (like in AD 70) or the end of human history as we know it (compare Matthew 24:13–14; see also Matthew 10:22; Matthew 13:39–40, Matthew 13:49).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: beginning of birth pains: God's people should expect intense suffering right before the second coming of Jesus (see also Mathhew 24:29–31; Isaiah 13:8; Isaiah 26:17; Jeremiah 4:31; Jeremiah 6:24; Micah 4:9–10).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: hated (see Acts 28:22): At the end of the first century, the Roman historian Tacitus described Christians as “the hated ones of mankind” (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). The suffering of righteous people sometimes has the purpose of encouraging repentance and obedience (see Exodus 4:31; Deuteronomy 4:30; Judges 10:6–16; Psalms 34:19; Psalms 37:39; Psalms 50:15).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Some people will stop being loyal to Jesus because of persecution (Matthew 10:25; Matthew 13:21; Matthew 16:24–28; Matthew 26:33).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: the love of most will grow cold (see Revelation 2:4): If the love within the community of the disciples of Jesus disappears, the community stops being what God designed it to be.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: the one who perseveres stays loyal to Jesus, even when persecuted. The end could mean the end of their life, the judgment on Israel in AD 70, or the end of history.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• in all the world: This points to the future mission to the Gentiles (see Matthew 21:43; Matthew 28:16–20). Before the end comes, there will be a time, whether short or long, when the good news spreads among the nations.

• Jesus said the end will be marked by three signs. First is "the abomination of desolation" (Matthew 24:15). Second is severe persecution (Matthew 24:16–28). Finally comes the sign of the Son of Man (Matthew 24:29–31).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• described by the prophet Daniel: He spoke about the desecration (or desolation) of the temple (see Daniel 8:13; Daniel 9:27; Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11). It would be made unclean and ruined.

• the abomination of desolation could be: 

• A false priest taking over the priesthood (see Josephus, War 4.3.6–10).

• Unlawful images of God or humans, or certain people who cannot be in the temple. These people would include Antiochus Epiphanes, Caligula, Vespasian, or Titus (see Josephus, War 4.4.1–4.7.1).

• The antichrist being present in the temple (compare 1 Maccabees 1:54–64; 2 Maccabees 8:17). The term "antichrist" refers to a person or teaching that opposes Jesus Christ and his work.

• let the reader understand: This hidden message shows a special connection between the writer and reader, based on a shared belief that these events fulfill the prophecies of Daniel 9, Daniel 11:11, and Daniel 12:12.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The Jewish historian Josephus records that the Jordan River swells in winter, making it harder to cross (see War 4.7.5). Muddy roads also made travel difficult in winter. 

• Jews usually did not travel on the Sabbath, so that they could rest as God commanded (see Genesis 2:1–3; Exodus 20:8–11; Exodus 23:12; Exodus 31:12–17; Leviticus 23:3; Deuteronomy 5:12–15; Jeremiah 17:19–27).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: great tribulation, unmatched: Similar language appears in Nehemiah 9:37; Jeremiah 11:16; Daniel 12:1; Joel 2:1–17. The Jewish historian Josephus documented the extreme violence of the times (see War 5.10.2–3).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: God's chosen people persevere (Matthew 24:13) and remain faithful (Matthew 24:37–25:46; see Isaiah 65:8–9; Romans 11:7).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• false Christs and false prophets (see Matthew 7:15; Matthew 24:4–8; also Acts 13:6; 2 Peter 2:1; 1 John 2:18; 1 John 4:1): Revelation describes a particular false prophet (see Revelation 16:13). 

• signs and wonders: Not all miracles are proof of God's approval (see Deuteronomy 13:1–4; Revelation 13:13).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Some Jewish prophets persuaded people to follow them into the desert to witness signs of salvation (see Matthew 24:4–8). 

• in the inner rooms: This might refer to secretive groups, like those at Qumran, or small fellowship groups linked to the Pharisees.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: These verses expand on Matthew 24:23. Jews debated where and how the Messiah would appear. The Messiah's glorious arrival and vindication will be clear to everyone.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Lightning here may point to the great cosmic signs that will mark the coming of the Messiah (see Matthew 24:29–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). The focus is on how easy the lightning is to see, not how suddenly it comes. Jesus probably shared these teachings to prevent early excitement about the end of time (1 Thessalonians 4:13–5:10; 2 Thessalonians 2:1–12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: ‘The sun will be darkened … the heavens will be shaken.’: This could be literal, as is fitting for a dramatic revelation of God's Son. Or, it could be a metaphor for a major cosmic event (see Acts 2:17–21; Hebrews 12:26–27; 2 Peter 3:10; Revelation 6:12–13). The Old Testament often uses similar apocalyptic language to describe political disasters and the collapse of governments as cosmic judgments from God (for example, Isaiah 13:9–16; Ezekiel 32:1–10; Joel 2:1–17; Amos 8:7–10).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
These sayings indicate the most important part of the discussion and answer the second question the disciples asked (see Matthew 24:3). Some believe Matthew 24:29–31 describes God's judgment on the Jewish people in AD 70. In this view, the apocalyptic images and metaphors picture the destruction of Jerusalem.

Others see these verses as pointing to the second coming of Christ at the end of history.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• the sign of the Son of Man: The sign is probably the Son of Man himself (see Matthew 12:38–42; Matthew 16:4). His coming shows that God has vindicated him (proved him right; see Matthew 26:64). It will also cause deep mourning for those who face God’s judgment.

• all the tribes of the earth: This could also mean "all the tribes of the land." The Greek term used here (phulai) often refers to the tribes of Israel. It is not the usual term for Gentiles (ethnoi). This suggests that it may refer to a national disaster in Israel (see Matthew 21:43; Zechariah 12:10–14). 

• the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven: See Daniel 7:13. Many think this means the Son of Man will descend from God's presence to live on earth as judge and savior. This is the second coming of Christ. Others believe it describes the Son of Man coming in judgment, but not necessarily as the second coming of Christ (see Matthew 10:23; Matthew 16:27; Matthew 19:28; Matthew 25:31; Matthew 26:64; Matthew 28:18).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Some believe this passage predicts the rapture, when God’s people are gathered by angels (Matthew 13:41; Matthew 16:27; Matthew 25:31). Others think the word angeloi (Greek for “messengers”) here refers to human messengers (Matthew 11:10; Luke 7:24; Luke 9:52; James 2:25). In this view, Jesus is describing the spread of the good news among the Gentiles (see Matthew 21:33–46; Matthew 22:1–14; Deuteronomy 30:1–10; Isaiah 27:13; Zechariah 2:6–13).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• all these things: This refers to events connected to the destruction of the temple. This phrase is first used in Matthew 23:36 (see Matthew 24:2, Matthew 24:8). 

• He is near (or it is near): It could mean the return of Jesus (see James 5:9; Revelation 3:20), the destruction of the temple, or the end of history (see Luke 21:31).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: this generation: In Matthew, generation refers particularly to the current Jews who do not trust in Jesus. This focuses especially on the leaders who have tried to make the people reject the Messiah (Matthew 11:16; Matthew 12:39, Matthew 12:41–42, Matthew 12:45; Matthew 16:4; Matthew 23:36).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The words of Jesus are as reliable as the words of God (see Matthew 5:18; Isaiah 40:8; Isaiah 55:11; Isaiah 59:21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• That day is the day of judgment. 

• nor the Son: This phrase shows that Jesus did not know the exact time. Acts 1:7 suggests the same idea. Because no one knows the day, Jesus told his followers to stay watchful and faithful (see Matthew 24:37–25:46). This statement should discourage anyone from trying to calculate the exact date when our Lord will return.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• at the coming of the Son of Man: This refers to the second coming of Jesus (see Matthew 24:3; compare Luke 17:26). 

• in the days of Noah (see Genesis 6:9–22; 2 Peter 2:5; 2 Peter 3:5–6): This is not comparing how serious the sins were. Instead, it shows that people did not notice what God was doing. They were too focused on everyday pleasures and celebrations (Matthew 6:19–34).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The second coming of Jesus will surprise people, just like the flood of Noah did (Genesis 7). The only way to be ready is to live consistently alert and obedient (compare Luke 17:26–27, Luke 17:34–35).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus now applied his prophecies (Matthew 24:1–36) to his disciples so they would stay faithful and be ready for his second coming.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The word taken most likely means taken in judgment, either in AD 70 or at the end of history. Left would then mean remaining to enter a new time. This new time could be the age of the church (see Matthew 21:43; Matthew 22:1–14) or the thousand–year reign of Christ on earth (the Millennium).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: keep watch: This means to actively and energetically obey the Lord with a single focus (see Matthew 25:13; Matthew 26:38–41).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: servant: Those who were listening to Jesus might have thought of God's special servants, the prophets and lawgivers. But Jesus often used servant as a metaphor, so it is likely he was describing every disciple's responsibility (see Matthew 10:24–25; Matthew 13:27–28; Matthew 18:23–35; Matthew 20:26).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This parable and the next three dramatize the importance of faithfully obeying while waiting for Jesus to return (Matthew 25:1–13, Matthew 25:14–30, Matthew 25:31–46).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• to meet the bridegroom: This image points to the coming of the Messiah (see Mark 2:19–20). 

• We do not know the exact wedding customs of that time. Some believe the bridesmaids led the bride to the bridegroom's home. He stayed away until the wedding feast began. The bridesmaids would wait for his arrival and then escort him to the feast (Matthew 25:10). 

Others think the bridegroom might have arrived late at night at the bride’s home, where they announced him. After celebrating with the bride’s guests, the groom would take his bride to his home under torches or lamps.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This parable confirms the need to be alert and ready for Christ's return (Matthew 25:13; see also Luke 12:35–36).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Some people think the oil represents something specific (such as the Holy Spirit). But it more likely emphasizes the need to prepare for Christ's second coming.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Both the prudent and the foolish bridesmaids sleep while waiting. The parable criticizes only the foolish bridesmaids’ failure to bring enough oil.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The bridegroom arriving at midnight while the bridesmaids slept makes a further point: the second coming of Jesus will be sudden and unexpected (Matthew 14:42–51).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This parable teaches that the Lord expects his servants to be faithful to the task given to them while waiting for his return. The delay of Christ’s return will cause some to do evil things (Matthew 24:48–49), some to become inactive (Matthew 25:3), and others may become fearfully passive (Matthew 25:18).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: After a long time: This emphasizes the long wait for Christ's return (Matthew 24:45–51).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• See Matthew 24:45–51; Luke 16:10. 

• Enter into the joy of your master!: This shows the Father’s approval. It may also point to the Messiah’s great banquet (see Matthew 6:1, Matthew 6:4, Matthew 6:6, Matthew 6:18; Matthew 9:9–17).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: I knew that you are a hard man: This servant uses a false understanding of his master as an excuse for being lazy.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: God gives plenty of grace to those who are faithful with what they already have (see Matthew 13:12).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: sit on His glorious throne: This represents a position of judgment (see Matthew 19:28; Matthew 22:44; Daniel 7:13–14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This describes the final judgment of which Jesus had been warning (see Matthew 7:13–27; Matthew 8:10–12; Matthew 11:20–24; Matthew 12:38–42; Matthew 13:24–30, Matthew 13:36–43; Matthew 16:24–28; Matthew 24:37–25:30).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: His right hand: This is a place of honor (Genesis 48:13–20; Psalm 110:1).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: prepared for you from the foundation of the world: This phrase might be a reference to God choosing people for salvation before time began (see Matthew 13:10–17; Ephesians 1:4; Revelation 17:8). Or it might only refer to the God's kingdom as a place (compare Matthew 25:41).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The actions mentioned here are often called "deeds of mercy." These were acts of kindness toward those in need (see Isaiah 58:1–12; Ezekiel 18:7; James 1:26–27). These good deeds are not efforts to earn God's approval. Instead, they come from a love for Christ that results in compassion toward others (see Matthew 6:1–4).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: These righteous people (see Mathhew 5:6, Matthew 5:20) obey God's will as Jesus taught them. They show this most clearly through acts of love (Matthew 7:12; Matthew 9:9–13; Matthew 22:34–40; Matthew 25:35–40).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: these brothers of Mine: This phrase may show the close bond Jesus had with his disciples (see Matthew 10:42; Matthew 18:1–14; Galatians 6:10). Or it could refer to all humanity, regardless of their faith (see Matthew 6:1–4; Matthew 25:43; Proverbs 19:17). The phrase brothers of Mine suggests the first meaning (Matthew 12:46–50; Matthew 18:15–35; Matthew 23:8; Matthew 28:10). But it does not exclude the duty to care for others in general (see Luke 10:30–37).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
The Greek word for eternal can mean "lasting forever" or "lasting for an age." It refers to "the age to come" (Matthew 13:39–40, Matthew 13:49; Matthew 24:3; John 17:3; 2 Thessalonians 1:9; Philemon 1:15; 1 John 5:11, 1 John 5:13). 

Some hope that the punishment of the damned will end after "an age." God will either destroy or forgive them. Yet, the comparison between eternal life and eternal punishment strongly suggests it means "lasting forever." This is because eternal life does not end (see also Luke 16:19–31; Hebrews 6:2; Revelation 20:10).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The irony is that the Son of Man, who will one day judge the nations (Matthew 25:31–46), must first be unfairly judged and condemned to death by evil people. The death of Jesus was the ultimate Passover sacrifice (see John 19:31–37; 1 Corinthians 5:7).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Caiaphas was the high priest. He lived near the temple in Jerusalem's upper city. This meeting was not at the usual place or time, so it was urgent and probably secret. The Sanhedrin (the official Jewish council) usually met in the council chamber. The council chamber was located either at the southern end of the court of the Israelites in the temple or on the western edge of the temple hill. 

• Joseph Caiaphas was the son-in-law of Annas (see John 18:13). He served as high priest from AD 18 to 36 (John 11:49). He had the longest term of any high priest from Herod's rule until AD 70. They had removed Annas, his father-in-law, from his position but he was still called high priest as well (see Luke 3:2; John 18:13, John 18:19–24).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: At Passover, Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims. The Jewish leaders feared losing their authority if they caused or permitted anything that looked like a revolt against Rome (see Matthew 21:8–11, Matthew 21:14–16).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Simon was a man who had once suffered from leprosy. Jesus being in his home showed the forgiving and healing love that Jesus often gave to people who were outcasts (see Matthew 8:7; Matthew 9:10).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: A similar anointing happened earlier in Galilee (Luke 7:36–50). Matthew includes this event here (compare John 12:1–8) to highlight different responses to Jesus. While the Jewish leaders were plotting to kill Jesus (Matthew 26:3–5) and Judas was preparing to betray him (Matthew 26:14–16), the woman honored Jesus with her actions.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The jar of costly perfume was used for burial customs (see Mark 16:1; Luke 23:56–24:1; John 12:1–7; John 19:38–42). It was made from nard, a plant harvested in India. The perfume was worth almost a full year’s wages(John 12:5).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: they were indignant: John 12:4 shows that Judas Iscariot caused this reaction.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: prepared My body for burial: We do not know if the woman fully understood what she was doing. The anointing also symbolizes Jesus as king and priest (1 Samuel 10:1; 2 Kings 9:6; Exodus 29:7).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
Judas sold himself to the authorities (see also John 11:57), kept it secret (Matthew 26:25), and led them to Jesus at the right time to arrest him (Matthew 26:47–56; see John 18:2). Later, feeling guilty, Judas killed himself (Matthew 27:3–10; see Acts 1:15–22). 

Judas was known for his greed (Matthew 26:14–15; John 12:4–6; John 13:29). Some think he may also have been disappointed in the kind of Messiah Jesus was, ashamed after the anointing of Jesus (see John 12:1–8). Others think he may have been resentful of the leadership of Peter, James, and John. Whatever his reasons, Judas’s betrayal was still part of God’s larger plan (Acts 1:16–17).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: My time: The Messiah would now complete the work for which he was commissioned, to die for the sins of the world.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: dipped his hand into the bowl with Me: Everyone would dip their food into a shared bowl, which probably had herbs and fruit puree in it. Sharing a meal showed friendship and trust, so having a betrayer there was shocking (Matthew 26:21; but see John 13:26).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: as it is written: Jesus might have been referring to Isaiah 53:7–9 or the broader Old Testament theme of a suffering Messiah. This verse shows both God's sovereign will and human responsibility.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Judas referred to Jesus as Rabbi, but the other disciples call him "Lord" (Mathhew 26:22). 

• You have said it yourself: This mysterious statement confirmed that Judas was the betrayer.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Deuteronomy 16:3 calls the unleavened bread of the Passover (see Exodus 12:18) the "bread of affliction." This is because it symbolizes the hardships in Egypt. 

• During the Passover meal, the traditional blessing over the bread is: "Blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth."

entries.title: Matthew
Matthew
entries.content:
• gave thanks: The traditional blessing for the Passover cup was “Blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who creates the fruit of the vine.” An early Christian version is “We give thanks to you, our Father, for the Holy Vine of David, your child, whom you revealed to us through Jesus your child; glory be to you forever” (Didache 9.2). 

• The four cups of the Passover meal match the four promises in Exodus 6:6–7: two for deliverance, one for redemption (see Matthew 26:27–28), and one for fellowship (see Matthew 26:29).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• the covenant: In God’s covenant with Israel, the blood of sheep or goats was shed and put on the doorposts at Passover (Exodus 12:5, Exodus 12:13; Exodus 24:8). They put it on the "the sides and tops of the doorframes" (Exodus 12:7). Jesus, the sinless Lamb of God, created a new covenant with his blood (see Jeremiah 31:31). The covenant represents God's self-initiated promise to bring salvation to humanity, fulfilling the promise to the patriarch Abraham (see Genesis 12; Galatians 3:15–29; Galatians 4:12–31). 

• for many for the forgiveness of sins: Jesus shed his blood as a sacrifice to forgive sins (see Jeremiah 31:31–34; Mark 14:24). Some think many means only God's chosen people, while others believe it means "all" (compare Matthew 20:28).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• until that day: The kingdom of God began with the ministry of Jesus, but it is not yet complete. It still awaits its full completion at the end (see 1 Corinthians 15:20–28; Revelation 19–22). 

• until that day when I drink it anew: Jesus describes the final completion of the kingdom as a great feast, like the Passover. This picture shows eternal fellowship with God and his people, marked by love and peace.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: when they had sung a hymn: Some people think they sang the Great Hallel (Psalm 136).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: I will strike: In Zechariah 13:7–9, a sword strikes God's partner, the Shepherd. Jesus understood this as a prophecy of his own death. From the scattered sheep, a purified group of faithful ones will emerge (Zechariah 13:8–9). In the short term, the disciples would soon scatter and deny knowing Jesus (Matthew 26:34, Matthew 26:56, Matthew 26:69–75).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus prophesied a time when the disciples would return, even though they were about to leave him (see chapter Matthew 28; John 21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Peter’s denial is the most well-known. But all the other disciples also left Jesus or avoided being connected with him (see Matthew 26:56).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Gethsemane is an olive orchard about 229 meters (about 250 yards) east of Jerusalem's Golden Gate. It is above the Kidron Valley on the Mount of Olives. Jesus and his disciples often met there (Luke 22:39–40; John 18:1–2).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This scene reveals how deeply Jesus understood the suffering he would encounter on the cross. It also reveals his complete dedication to God's will (see Matthew 20:28). The words in Matthew 26:41–42 echo the Lord’s Prayer in Matthew 6:9–13.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• He took with Him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee: Peter, James, and John were probably the leaders of the apostles. They received special revelation (Peter, James, and John were present at the Transfiguration, where they saw Jesus transformed on the mountain, Matthew 17:1–13). They stayed with Jesus during this difficult time. 

• Jesus felt sorrow and distress as he thought about the Father’s plan for him (see Matthew 27:45–46). Though he had never sinned, Jesus would take on humanity’s sin so that people could become "the righteousness of God" in Jesus (2 Corinthians 5:21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: consumed with sorrow: See John 12:27; compare with Psalms 42:5–6, Psalms 42:11; Psalms 43:5.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• if it is possible: Jesus desired to obey the Father fully while dreading the suffering and judgment he was about to bear.

• Yet not as I will, but as You will: He continued to do the Father's will (Matthew 4:1–11; Matthew 16:23; John 6:38).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: kissed Him: Judas used a sign of friendship to betray Jesus. This makes his betrayal even worse.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: one of Jesus’ companions: This was Peter (John 18:26).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: twelve legions: Jesus used Roman military language to describe the help he could receive from God. A legion was about 6,000 soldiers. Jesus was not a helpless victim. He allowed his own arrest.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: If Jesus had resisted, it would have blocked the fulfillment of God’s saving work (see Matthew 16:21–23).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The leaders acted secretly because they feared the people who honored Jesus (see Matthew 21:26, Matthew 21:46; Matthew 26:3–5).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• We do not know which of the Scriptures Jesus was referring to. It might have been Isaiah 53 or the general Old Testament theme of a suffering Messiah. 

• As Jesus had predicted earlier that evening, all the disciples adandoned him (Matthew 26:31–35).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This hearing was probably an informal meeting to agree on the charges. The Jewish leaders faced pressure to keep the hearing secret to avoid a riot (see Matthew 21:26, Matthew 21:46; Matthew 26:5, Matthew 26:55; John 11:45–53).

entries.title: Matthew
Matthew
entries.content: the courtyard of the high priest: This place indicates an unplanned meeting of the Sanhedrin at the high priest's palace (Matthew 26:3).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: were seeking false testimony: The verb tense suggests a long and possibly desperate attempt to find any testimony to support a formal accusation (see Mark 14:55–56).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: they did not find any: This was because the evidence was too weak or inconsistent to seek a death sentence. This changed when two men gave testimonies that matched (Deuteronomy 17:6; Deuteronomy 19:15).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The charge was either a misunderstanding or a deliberate misrepresentation of what Jesus had said about his death and resurrection (see John 2:19–21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: if You are the Christ: The high priest asked this because Zechariah 6:12 prophesied that the Christ (Messiah) would rebuild the temple (compare Matthew 26:61).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• You have said it yourself: This was a careful but clear “yes” (see Matthew 26:25; Matthew 27:11). In Mark’s account Jesus answers, “I Am” (Mark 14:62). 

• you will see: By quoting Daniel 7:13, Jesus confirmed he was the Son of Man who God would vindicate and honor.

• sitting at the right hand of Power: See Psalm 110:1. Jews often avoided saying God's name directly (see study note on Matthew 5:4). 

• The phrase coming on the clouds of heaven might refer to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 or to the return of Jesus at the end of history.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: He has blasphemed: Caiaphas thought Jesus had spoken against God (blasphemed) when Jesus claimed to be the Son of Man. The title "Son of Man" was very special. It described someone who shared God's glory and power (Daniel 7:13–14).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This abuse fulfills the prophecies in Isaiah 50:6 and Isaiah 53:4–9. Jesus himself prophesied these things (Matthew 16:21; Matthew 17:22–23; Matthew 20:18–19; Matthew 26:2; see also Mark 14:65).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Peter's denials fulfill what Jesus prophesied (Matthew 26:34).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: your accent: Jews from Galilee spoke with a distinct accent compared to those from Judea (see Matthew 4:13 and the related study note).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The crow of the rooster reminded Peter of what Jesus predicted would happen (Matthew 26:34). Peter felt deep sorrow.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Jewish leaders said Jesus had spoken blasphemy (Matthew 26:65–66). That charge was enough for the death penalty under Jewish law, but it would not persuade a Roman judge. So the leading priests and elders worked together to create a political charge that would fit Roman law on capital offenses (see Matthew 27:11–26; Luke 23:2).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Jewish leaders prepared charges against Jesus so that Pilate would order his death. Pilate, a Gentile, fulfills the prediction of Jesus from Matthew 20:19.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Tiberius Caesar made Pilate the governor (or prefect) of Judea. Pilate mainly governed from Caesarea, not Jerusalem, from AD 26 to AD 36. Although he had full power in Judea, Pilate answered to the governor (or legate) of Syria. This man was the main authority in the eastern Roman Empire. The Jewish historian Josephus records several mentions of Pilate. Pilate's disrespect for the holiness of Jewish customs caused revolts.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Judas felt deep remorse (the Greek word metamelomai), but he did not repent (the Greek word metanoeō). Repentance would have changed his heart and led to obedience and a relationship with God through faith.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
There are two stories about Judas's death. This one and the one found in Acts 1:18–19. There are differences between the two stories:

• Matthew says the priests bought the field (Matthew 27:6–7), but Acts suggests Judas bought it (Acts 1:18). 

• Matthew says Judas hanged himself by hanging (Matthew 27:5). Acts says he fell and his body burst open (Acts 1:18).

• Matthew says the field of blood was named for its use as a burial place (Matthew 27:7–8). Acts says it was named because of Judas’s violent death (Acts 1:19). 

The stories can align if Acts describes the results of Matthew's events.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: innocent blood: The innocence of Jesus is a key theme in the story of his suffering (see Matthew 23:35; Matthew 26:55–56, Matthew 26:59–60; Matthew 27:18–19, Matthew 27:24; see also Luke 23:47).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: hanged himself: Judas killed himself because he felt guilty but did not repent. His death also matched the Old Testament law about punishing a false witness (see Deuteronomy 19:16–21).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: foreigners: These were non-Jewish people who died in Jerusalem. If they could not find the owner of donated money, they used it for public charity. In this case, they used money considered ceremonially unclean to buy a ceremonially unclean place for people considered ceremonially unclean.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Field of Blood: This is another way of describing a cemetery (compare Acts 1:18–19).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled: The quote is from Zechariah 11:12–13. Matthew might have followed the Jewish tradition of naming books by the first book in the scroll. In this case, Jeremiah would be the first book in the scroll containing Zechariah. Or, Matthew might be referencing similar passages in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 19:1–13; Jeremiah 18:2–6; Jeremiah 32:6–15) along with Zechariah 11:12–13. 

• Matthew notices a strong similarity between Zechariah's actions and those of the leading priests. Both situations involve rejecting God's messenger, who was meant to be the king of God's people.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: King of the Jews: The Sanhedrin's first charge of blasphemy in Matthew 26:65–66; Matthew 27:1 did not cause concern for the Romans. The Romabs considered it to be a Jewish religious issue (see Acts 25:18–20). So, the Sanhedrin changed the charge to make Jesus seem like a political rebel to the Romans (see Luke 23:2).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Roman trial included an initial hearing before Pilatee (Matthew 27:11–14), then one before Herod Antipas (Luke 23:6–16), and a second hearing with Pilate (Matthew 27:15–26).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Pilate's behavior seems unusual. It was not normal for him to try to please his Jewish subjects. But Pilate's relationship with Caesar might have been unstable at this time (see study note on John 19:12; see Philo, On the Embassy to Gaius 159–161). If so, this gesture might have been to maintain peace and avoid negative attention from Rome.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: notorious prisoner named Barabbas: He is also called an "insurrectionist" (Mark 15:7; John 18:40). This word can also mean a robber or someone who led a revolt (see Luke 23:19). To the zealots, Barabbas was considered a hero.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: have suffered terribly in a dream (compare Matthew 1:20): It is notable that a pagan woman recognized Jesus innocence and spoke up for him, while the Jewish crowd did not.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: You bear the responsibility: The priests told Judas the same thing (Matthew 27:4).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• All the people (see Matthew 21:43): This does not mean every living Jewish person. Instead, it refers to those who urged the condemnation of Jesus. They represented all of Israel who disbelieved Jesus. Their actions led to consequences for the entire nation, like the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. 

• His blood be on us and on our children! (see Matthew 23:35; 2 Samuel 1:16; 2 Samuel 14:9; Jeremiah 51:35; Acts 5:28; Acts 18:6; Acts 20:26): Some Christians have misunderstood and misused this verse as a basis for persecuting Jews. But it is not a general accusation against all Jewish people.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: When the Romans flogged a man, they beat him with whips that had leather straps on the end. Some straps had sharp bone, lead, or rock pieces attached (see also Deuteronomy 25:1–3; 1 Kings 12:11, 1 Kings 12:14; Acts 16:22; Acts 22:25; 2 Corinthians 11:24–25).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• the governor's soldiers were extra troops recruited from non-Jewish residents of Palestine. 

• The soldiers stayed at the governor's official building in Jerusalem. This building was called the Antonia Fortress. It stood at the northwest corner of the Temple area.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: During the Jewish trial, people mocked Jesus as a prophet (Matthew 26:67–68). Here, they mocked him as a king.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The scarlet robe was probably a soldier's cloak used to imitate royal clothing in order to mock Jesus. 

• Weaving a crown of thorns was meant to mock Jesus as a king.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Usually, the person to be crucified would carry their own cross. They only carried the crossbeam since the vertical pole was already at the crucifixion site. The Romans might have forced Simon to help because Jesus was weak from being whipped. Making Simon help could also have been a way to mock Jesus. They treated him like someone who deserved a servant, even though they led him to his death.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The crowd mocked Jesus, but their words were still true. He is the Son of God, the King of Israel, and the Messiah.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• They probably gave Jesus wine mixed with bitter gall to ridicule him (see Psalm 69:21). It also was a sedative. Jesus probably refused it so he could fully experience suffering for our sins (see Isaiah 53:10). 

• Gall is another name sometimes given to wormwood. It is a very bitter substance made from the oil of the Artemisia plant, sometimes used as medicine in the ancient world (compare Mark 15:23).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
they had crucified Him: Crucifixion (being nailed to a cross) was not common among Jews. But it was a widespread Roman punishment for military and political offenders. This was especially true for slaves, rebels, and insurrectionists (rioters). The extreme cruelty and public display of crucifixion was a strong warning to society. 

The Romans would flog victims (beat them with whips). Then they would crucify the victims naked. This added to their humiliation. Most considered it the most painful death possible. It involved intense suffering, exposure to weather and insects, and suffocation. It often concluded with a final violent spear thrust to end life. 

Since the Law said that anyone hung on a tree was under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), crucifixion was especially offensive to the Jewish people. Yet in God’s plan, what humans saw as shameful became the very means of salvation. Earlier, Jesus had told his disciples to take up their cross and follow him (Matthew 16:24).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The Romans would fasten the official crime to the cross above the head of the offender. They accused Jesus of political rebellion.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Jesus was crucified between two convicted revolutionaries. This increased his shame and made him appear guilty by association (linked with rebels).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: If You are the Son of God: This taunt reminds us of when the devil tempted Jesus at the start of his public ministry (Matthew 4:1–11). The devil tried to use the special status of Jesus to tempt him to avoid suffering (see also Matthew 16:21–23).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: darkness: This represents God's judgment. Or, it could more specifically refer to the coming of the day of the Lord (see Amos 5:18, Amos 5:20; Amos 8:9–10; also Jeremiah 4:27–28; Jeremiah 13:16; Jeremiah 15:9).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Eli, Eli: This cry means My God, My God. The sound of these words may have made some people think Jesus was calling for Elijah (Matthew 27:47). 

• My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?: Jesus was expressing the weight of judgment he bore for humanity’s sin.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Many Jews believed Elijah would return before the day of the Lord (Matthew 11:14–15; Matthew 17:10–13; Malachi 4:5).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The sour wine was vinegar. The drink was probably meant to mock Jesus by pretending to ease his thirst (compare Psalm 69:21 with Matthew 27:34). Although some scholars think they offered it as a genuine act of kindness.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Each of the four gospels focuses on different parts of the final moments of Jesus. 

• He yielded up His spirit: Jesus gave up his life willingly. This shows his authority, since he chose the moment of his own death (see also John 19:30). 

• Jesus had cried out again (see Matthew 27:46): This final loud cry was the last prayer of Jesus (see Luke 23:46).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The tearing of the temple curtain is symbolic. It means that that the wall dividing people from God has been torn down by the death of Jesus (see also Ephesians 2:11–22; Hebrews 6:19; Hebrews 9:1–10:25). 

• The earth quaked and the rocks were split: These are signs that judgment has come (see Exodus 19:18; Judges 5:4; Psalm 18:7; Joel 3:14–17; Amos 8:8–10). The Jewish historian Josephus records that around AD 30, a star resembling a sword appeared and the temple gates opened by themselves (Josephus, War 6.5.3–4).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The tombs broke open: At the moment of the death of Jesus, God’s kingdom broke into the world in a new way. His death destroyed the power of death and began the promise of final resurrection (see Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2; 1 Corinthians 15:1–58; Colossians 1:18; Hebrews 2:14–15). 

• Some holy people were raised to life. But they may not have entered Jerusalem until after Jesus rose from the dead. Another view is that they were not raised until after the resurrection of Jesus, since Jesus is the “firstfruits” (the first to be raised, showing what will come for others; see 1 Corinthians 15:20, 1 Corinthians 15:23; Colossians 1:18). If this second view is correct, Matthew included the story to show the great impact of the death of Jesus.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• The Roman officer and the other soldiers were not Jewish. 

• the Son of God: This could be a clear statement that Jesus is the unique Son of God (see Matthew 14:33; Matthew 16:16) or perhaps a general statement about the innocence of Jesus (see Luke 23:47). They reacted to the earthquake and everything that happened as signs of divine involvement in this event.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• In Roman crucifixion, the bodies of criminals were often left on the cross until they rotted. Jewish law, however, did not allow this. Deuteronomy 21:22–23 forbids leaving a body on a cross or gallows overnight. Joseph of Arimathea acted in line with this law when he asked for the body of Jesus. His request also showed his loyalty to Jesus.

• Pilate ordered: Pilate agreed to Joseph’s request and gave the order. He likely did this because he did not believe Jesus was guilty of rebellion against Rome (see Matthew 27:24–26).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Burial customs were important in Judaism, unlike the Greeks and Romans who cremated their dead. Jews considered leaving a body unburied to be a severe punishment (Deuteronomy 21:22–23; 2 Kings 9:37; Psalm 79:3; Jeremiah 16:4, Jeremiah 16:6; Ezekiel 29:5; Revelation 11:9). 

People mourned and lamented death (Mark 5:38–39). They washed the body (Acts 9:37). They anointed the body (Matt 26:6–13; John 12:3, John 12:7; John 19:39). And they wrapped the body in burial cloths (Matthew 27:59; see Genesis 50:2–3). Then they placed the body in a tomb (Matthew 23:27). This tomb was either tunneled into rock or carved into a cave wall. A large stone often sealed the tomb to prevent ceremonial uncleanness or stealing. 

• clean linen … new tomb: These terms symbolize ceremonial purity. Joseph of Arimathea bought the tomb for his family, but had not used it.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: This event supports the truth of Jesus resurrection. It is very unlikely that Matthew invented the story, because many witnesses were alive who could have denied it.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: Mary Magdalene (see Matthew 27:56): Mentioning two women as witnesses adds credibility to the story. In those times, people considered the testimony of a woman less reliable than a man. So a someone making up a false story would not have chosen women as witnesses.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
The four gospels each emphasize different aspects of the empty tomb and resurrection appearances. Matthew focuses on three things: 

• the reunion of Jesus and his disciples in Galilee, 

• the Jewish leaders' attempt to discredit the resurrection, and 

• the importance of the ressurection for the salvation of the world.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• Such a bribe was against the law (see Exodus 20:16; Exodus 23:8). 

• elders: See the study note on Matthew 21:23.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: stole him away: Stealing from tombs was common in ancient times. So this accusation would have been easy to believe.

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
And this account has been circulated among the Jews to this very day: Around AD 165, the early church father Justin Martyr wrote to the Jews of his time. He wrote, “You have sent . . . men throughout all the world to proclaim, ‘A godless and lawless heresy has sprung from one Jesus, a Galilean deceiver, whom we crucified, but his disciples stole him by night from the tomb . . . and now [the disciples] deceive men by asserting that he has risen from the dead and ascended into heaven’” (Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 108). 

This false information probably increased after the disciples began preaching about the resurrection of Jesus (see Acts 2:22–36).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: some doubted: This could refer to Thomas (John 20:24–29). But all eleven disciples might have experienced mixed feelings of worship and doubt (see also Matt 14:31; Luke 24:10–11; John 20:24–29).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: The authority of Jesus comes from the power given to him by the Father (see Matthew 7:29; Matthew 9:6–8; Matthew 21:23–27; Matthew 26:64; John 3:35).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content:
• go and (literally going): This is a command to make disciples. Matthew likely meant "go" as a separate command, not just as "while you go"(compare similar uses in Matthew 9:6; Acts 10:20). 

• make disciples: A disciple turns from sin, trusts Jesus for salvation, and obeys his teachings. 

• all nations: The gospel mission to non-Jewish (Gentile) people officially started here (see Matthew 10:5–6; Matthew 15:24; also Matthew 1:1; Matthew 2:1–12; Matthew 8:5–13; Matthew 21:43; Matthew 24:14; Matthew 26:13). 

• Two parts of making disciples are baptizing and teaching (Matthew 28:20). Baptism is a public identification with Jesus and submission to him and his work of salvation (see Matthew 3:13–17; Matthew 10:32–33; Matthew 20:28; Matthew 26:28; Acts 2:38; Romans 6:1–11; 1 Peter 3:21). 

• in the name of: This means entering a relationship and its benefits for true believers in Christ. 

• Father … Son … Holy Spirit: This phrase shows the Christian belief that the one God is three persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) known as the Trinity (see also 1 Corinthians 12:4–6; 2 Corinthians 13:14; Ephesians 4:4–6; 2 Thessalonians 2:13–14; 1 Peter 1:2; Revelation 1:4–6).

entries.title: Matthew
entries.content: teaching: The disciples are to teach people everything Jesus commanded, such as the Sermon on the Mount (chapters Matthew 5:5–7). People should recognize the church because it obeys the commands of Jesus (Matthew 5:17–20; Matthew 7:13–27). The authority and presence of Jesus establish the mission of the disciples (see also Matthew 1:23; Matthew 18:20).
